paper.title: Magnetoelectric Wireless Power Transfer Receivers for Sub-Millimeter Scale Implantable Bioelectronics
paper.abstract: Implanted biomedical devices for continuous physiological monitoring require reliable wireless power delivery to anatomically constrained and sensitive sites where batteries are impractical or hazardous. Existing wireless power transfer (WPT) modalities, including inductive coils and ultrasonic transducers suffer from performance degradation as receiver dimensions are miniaturized, limiting their application for space-limited locations such as fingertips, the ocular cavity, and intracranial sites. We present a microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) magnetoelectric WPT receiver integrating piezoelectric aluminum scandium nitride and magnetostrictive iron-cobalt/silver multilayer thin-films, microfabricated within a footprint of 770 x 360 x 2.25 micrometers. The receiver operates at its 100 kHz flexural-mode resonance with a quality factor of 1180 and delivers 1.0 microwatt to a matched 10 kohm load under a standard-compliant 205 micro-Tesla RMS excitation field. This device exhibits a magnetoelectric coefficient of 1274 V cm-1 Oe-1 and a power figure of merit (FOMP) of 4.05 x 10-3 mW cm-3 Oe-2 Hz-1, both the highest reported values of comparable magnetoelectric WPT receivers. The FOM is 20-fold higher than the next best comparable-frequency device. These miniaturized devices establish MEMS magnetoelectric transduction as a scalable platform for battery-free wireless powering of microwatt-class implants in the most anatomically demanding regions of the body.

## Magnetoelectric Wireless Power Transfer Receivers for SubMillimeter Scale Implantable Bioelectronics 

Authors: Jonathan Tan[1] , Serene Feng[1] , Thomas Mion[2] , Sydney Acosta[1] , Konrad Bussmann[2] , Peter Finkel[2] , Roy Olsson[1*] 

1Department of Electrical and Systems Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA 

2Materials Science and Technology Division, US Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC 02375, USA 

*Email: rolsson@seas.upenn.edu 

## Abstract 

Implanted biomedical devices for continuous physiological monitoring require reliable wireless power delivery to anatomically constrained and sensitive sites where batteries are impractical or hazardous. Existing wireless power transfer (WPT) modalities, including inductive coils and ultrasonic transducers, su�er from performance degradation as receiver dimensions are miniaturized, limiting their application for space-limited locations such as fingertips, ocular cavity, and intracranial sites. We present a microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) magnetoelectric WPT receiver integrating piezoelectric aluminum scandium nitride and magnetostrictive iron-cobalt/silver multilayer thin-films, microfabricated within a footprint of 770 × 360 × 2.25 µm. The receiver operates at its 100 kHz flexural-mode resonance with a quality factor of 1180 and delivers 1.0 µW to a matched 10 kΩ load under a standard-compliant 205 µTRMS excitation field. This device exhibits a magnetoelectric coupling coe�icient of 1274 V cm[-1] Oe[-1] and a power figure of merit (FOMP) of 4.05 × 10[-3] mW cm[-3] Oe[-2] Hz[-1] , both the highest reported values of comparable magnetoelectric WPT receivers. The FOM is 20-fold higher than the next best comparablefrequency device. These miniaturized devices establish MEMS magnetoelectric transduction as a scalable platform for battery-free wireless powering of microwatt-class implants in the most anatomically demanding regions of the body.

## Introduction 

The biomedical internet-of-things envisions a future of wide-ranging implantable and wearable medical devices for continuous and remote measurement of biomarkers, providing valuable data for healthcare professionals to better diagnose and treat conditions[20, 21]. Commercially available medical devices such as pacemakers and continuous glucose monitors rely on an internal battery for power. These batteries can fail or require replacement over time, necessitating invasive surgeries[22, 23]. Biomedical devices implanted into anatomically constrained and sensitive sites, including those for peripheral nerve recording[24-26], brain neurotransmitter sensing[27], electrocardiography[28], blood flow monitoring[29], pressure sensing in the fingers[1], and intraocular and intracranial pressure[2, 30], all require power for operation while being severely restricted in overall system volume. For these devices, implanting them with a bulky battery is infeasible, as the proximity to sensitive organs limits the space available for implants. 

Wireless power transfer (WPT) o�ers the ability to continuously power implanted, batteryfree medical devices through an external stimulus[31, 32]. In anatomically sensitive locations such as the head and torso, the permitted incident power transmitted to the body is frequency-dependent and highly limited, necessitating thoughtful receiver design[33]. WPT receivers for implantation into space-constrained and sensitive sites should therefore exhibit high power density, through both minimal sizing and high coupling between the external stimulus power and the delivered electrical power. WPT receivers used in research and clinical bioelectronics operate based on several modalities, including inductive coupling, ultrasonic acoustics, and the magnetoelectric (ME) e�ect[31, 32]. 

Inductively coupled coils operate on the principle of electromagnetic induction, generating electrical current in a receiving coil through a time-varying magnetic field produced by a transmit coil. As the receiver dimensions decrease, the magnetic flux through the coil decreases, directly impacting power delivered to the load[32]. Additionally, inductive coils are inherently sensitive to misalignment and typically operate at MHz frequencies, at which the permissible whole-body magnetic field strength is significantly lower than at frequencies below 100 kHz, described by IEEE Std C95.1-2019[33, 34]. Although operating at lower frequencies enables higher magnetic-field strengths, it incurs a separate penalty of decreased coil quality factor (Q = ω L/R)[35]. Together, these constraints make inductive coils poorly suited for implanted devices in space-constrained locations where magnetic field strengths are highly limited. 

Ultrasonic WPT receivers o�er an alternative approach but introduce a distinct set of scaling limitations. Ultrasonic WPT receivers typically employ a resonant piezoelectric plate or diaphragm that generates a voltage upon displacement caused by acoustic waves generated 

outside the body[36]. As the dimensions decrease, the resonant frequency of the ultrasonic transducer increases. At these higher frequencies, biological tissues become increasingly absorptive to ultrasound energy[37]. To counteract the losses introduced by the absorptive tissue medium, higher incident power at the surface of the skin is required. The limits to diagnostic ultrasound power set by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) scale as f[-] 1/2, with excessive acoustic beam pressure risking cavitation in tissue[36]. Miniaturization of ultrasonic WPT transducers therefore simultaneously increases the incident power required to overcome tissue losses and reduces the maximum power permitted by FDA safety limits. 

The scaling limitations of WPT through inductive coupling and ultrasonic transduction motivate a magnetoelectric WPT approach, an alternative modality that operates with negligible losses to the body and without the performance penalties that accompany miniaturization of both inductive and ultrasonic WPT. ME WPT receivers operate through the strain-coupling of piezoelectric and magnetostrictive materials. In an external time-varying magnetic field, strain generated in the magnetostrictive layer is mechanically coupled to the piezoelectric layer, producing a time-varying voltage and delivering power to a load[38]. At low frequencies, magnetic field penetration through tissue is lossless and the permissible magnetic field strengths are high[33], allowing ME WPT receivers to avoid the fundamental scaling limitations that hamper inductive and ultrasonic WPT modalities at small dimensions. 

Piezoelectric materials transduce energy between mechanical and electrical domains, generating an electric field in response to applied stress. This response is described by 𝐷� = 𝑑��𝑇�, where Di is the electric displacement field in the i direction, dij is the piezoelectric coe�icient, and Tj is the stress applied in the j direction; materials with larger piezoelectric coe�icient produce a larger electric field for a given mechanical strain. Lead zirconate titanate (PZT) is a common piezoelectric material in ME WPT devices because of its high piezoelectric coe�icient[39-41]. Aluminum nitride (AlN) is common in micrometer-scale sensors and devices because of its intrinsic piezoelectricity and CMOS back-end-of-line compatibility[42-44]. Scandium substitution into the AlN lattice (AlScN) significantly enhances the piezoelectric coe�icient (d31) relative to pure AlN[45, 46]. Unlike PZT, AlScN is lead-free, making it more suitable for implantable applications by eliminating biocompatibility risks and bulky enclosures required when implanting PZT devices.[38, 41, 47]. AlScN is therefore used as the piezoelectric layer in this work. 

The performance of a ME WPT receiver depends equally on the properties of the magnetostrictive layer, which transduces energy between the applied AC magnetic field and mechanical strain. The piezomagnetic coe�icient, 𝑑��,� = 𝑑𝜆/𝑑𝐻, describes this response, the magnetostrictive strain (𝜆) generated per unit of applied magnetic field (𝐻), for a magnetic field and strain in the same direction[38]. The d33,m of a magnetostrictive material 

may be required to optimally bias the magnetostrictive layer to provide the largest d33,m response[38, 40]. In WPT applications, minimized optimal bias fields are desired, as the need for DC magnetic fields requires permanent magnets or electromagnets. Common magnetostrictive materials for WPT devices include iron-cobalt (FeCo) alloys[42], FeGaB[44], and Metglas[39-41]. Multilayers of Fe50Co50 and silver (Fe50Co50/Ag ML) have been shown to reduce the coercive field and increase the piezomagnetic coe�icient of the magnetostrictive film, as compared to a single layer of Fe50Co50[48]. Thin-film Fe50Co50/Ag ML is therefore used as the magnetostrictive material in this work. 

While centimeter and millimeter-scale ME WPT have demonstrated milliwatt-level power delivery[39, 49, 50], devices implanted in the most anatomically sensitive and constrained sites, such as neurotransmitter sensing in the brain[27] and pressure sensing in the fingertips[1] or eye[2], require at least an order of magnitude decrease in WPT receiver size. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), micro-scale devices that transform energy between electrical and mechanical domains, provide a path to this miniaturization, enabling ME WPT receivers with micrometer-scale dimensions through photolithography, deposition, and etching microfabrication techniques. Critically, high strain-coupling between magnetostrictive and piezoelectric materials can be achieved through the deposition of these materials directly onto one another without the use of mechanically lossy polymer adhesives used in larger ME WPT receivers[9, 50, 51]. Operation of a MEMS ME WPT receiver at its mechanical resonance amplifies the device velocity by its quality factor Q, describing the ratio of mechanical energy stored to the energy lost per cycle of its resonance. Output power delivered to a matched load increases linearly with the quality factor of the resonance, making Q a critical factor in the design of ME WPT receivers. The MEMS ME WPT receiver in this work demonstrates significant scaling benefits over inductive, ultrasonic, and macro-scale magnetoelectric WPT receivers in literature, as shown in Figure 1b. 

In this work, we present a MEMS ME WPT receiver with sub-millimeter dimensions of 770 × 360 × 2.25 µm, designed to operate at its 100 kHz flexural-mode resonance within the IEEE C95.1-2019 whole-body magnetic field safety limit[33]. The WPT receiver is able to deliver 1 µW of power to a matched resistive load, achieving record magnetoelectric coupling coe�icient and power figure of merit among comparable-frequency ME WPT receivers. With microwatt output power and sub-millimeter dimensions, this device is well suited to power sensors and bioelectronics in anatomically constrained sites including intraocular and fingertip pressure sensors[1, 2], and neural recorders and readout electronics[25, 52], as illustrated in Figure 1a. The results presented here establish MEMS ME transduction as a platform for battery-free wireless powering of implants in the most anatomically demanding and sensitive regions of the body. 

## Results 

## Flexural-Mode Resonator 

The MEMS ME WPT device was designed around the resonant frequency and allowable incident magnetic field at the skin. ME WPT receiver output power increases linearly with frequency and with the square of the excitation AC magnetic field[53], making the choice of operating frequency critical toward maximizing the power delivery of the device at safe magnetic field strengths. Magnetically actuating ME WPT receivers at 100 kHz takes advantage of the flat maximum whole-body magnetic field limit below 100 kHz before a decrease with 1/f above 100 kHz[33]. Operation at 100 kHz maximizes the product of permissible squared magnetic field and frequency, as shown in Supplementary Note 1. 

Achieving a mechanical resonance at 100 kHz in a sub-millimeter device requires careful resonant mode selection, as miniaturization generally increases resonant frequency. The flexural bending-mode resonance was chosen for its out-of-plane compliance, which yields a significantly lower resonant frequency than length- or width-extensional resonant modes of equivalent resonator dimensions[54]. A MEMS free-free beam geometry was designed to take advantage of this compliance, achieving approximately 100 kHz flexural-mode resonance while maintaining sub-millimeter dimensions. 

connected by 10 × 10 µm tethers, creating a total resonant structure dimension of 360 × 590 µm. Tethers of dimensions 10 × 90 µm anchor the free-free beams to the substrate at the quasi-nodal points of the flexural resonant mode, approximately halfway between the center and edge of the beam[55]. Anchoring at the quasi-nodal points minimizes anchor losses that dampen the motion of the resonating beams. A comparison between the size of the WPT device with a U.S. dime along with a scanning electron micrograph of the resonant structure is shown in Figure 1c. The material stack of the device from the intrinsic Si substrate includes 15 nm Ti / 150 nm Pt / 1 µm AlScN / 10 nm Ti / 100 nm Pt / 1 µm Fe50Co50/Ag ML, with the Fe50Co50/Ag multilayer only on the resonant beam area. The microfabrication flow is described in the methods section, with the cross-section fabrication flow depicted in Supplementary Note 5. The simulated flexural mode shape and surface stress distribution from a COMSOL eigenfrequency study are shown in Figure 2a, and an optical micrograph of the fabricated receiver showing the suspended resonant structure following isotropic XeF2 silicon release is shown in Figure 2b. 

The resonance of the WPT receiver was characterized by measuring the two-port S21 transmission S-parameter under 4 mBar vacuum using a network analyzer (Agilent Technologies E5061B). A modified-Butterworth van Dyke (mBVD) model was fit to the S21 measurement to extract the device parameters. The mBVD circuit model with fitted 

parameters is shown in Supplementary Note 2. The full S parameters were converted to admittance Y parameters, with the Y21 admittance plotted in Figure 2c along with the admittance of the fit mBVD model. The WPT receiver exhibits a resonant frequency of 98.825 kHz, a quality factor of 1180, an electromechanical coupling coe�icient, ke�[2] , of 0.55%, and an admittance of -79.89 dB, corresponding to a series resistance at resonance of 9.87 kΩ. 

The ME output of the receiver is partially governed by the piezomagnetic coe�icient, d33,m, of the magnetostrictive Fe50Co50/Ag ML, which is maximized at an optimal DC bias magnetic field. To identify this optimal bias, a DC magnetic field was swept using wound electromagnets while applying a 3.96 µTRMS AC magnetic field at the 98.8 kHz device resonance and measuring the device output into a 50 Ω power spectrum analyzer (full testing setup described in Methods). The magnetoelectric coupling coe�icient, 𝛼�� = 𝜕𝐸/𝜕𝐻= 𝑉��𝑡����𝐻����, describing the relationship between induced electric field across the piezoelectric layer and the applied AC magnetic field, was calculated from the measured output power and is plotted as a function of DC bias field in Figure 2d. The response exhibits a local minimum at 2 mT due to intrinsic hysteretic e�ects in the magnetostriction response, combined with residual stress in the magnetic layer[56]. The maximum of the magnetostriction response to the AC H-field was observed when the device was biased around 3.2 mT. However, upon saturating the magnetostrictive film at 6 mT and returning the bias field to lower magnitudes, the magnetostriction response increased and the optimal bias field shifted to 4 mT, as shown in Figure 2d. Unless otherwise stated, all experiments were performed after saturating the magnetic field at 6 mT and subsequently maintaining the bias field at 4 mT to optimally bias the magnetostrictive film. 

The ME coupling coe�icient was additionally determined from the open-circuit voltage of the WPT receiver. One port of the WPT receiver was connected to a SMA short standard, with the other port connected to the 1 MΩ / 15 pF input of a voltage spectrum analyzer (Stanford Research Systems SR770). The vacuum chamber was pumped to 4 mBar vacuum and 4 mT bias magnetic field was applied to the device. An AC magnetic field with magnitude of 0.396 µTrms was applied, and 0.464 mVRMS was measured in the spectrum analyzer. Correcting for the loading e�ect of the 15 pF input capacitance of the spectrum analyzer, the open-circuit voltage is calculated to be 0.5050 mVRMS, yielding a ME coupling coe�icient, 𝛼��, of 1274 V cm[-1] Oe[-1] for the 1 µm thick AlScN piezoelectric layer. This represents the highest ME coupling coe�icient reported among ME devices operating within an order of magnitude of this frequency[38, 42].

## Wireless Power Transfer 

While a MEMS ME device of comparable size has been reported in the literature, only ME coupling coe�icients were reported[42]. However, power delivery to a matched load under realistic magnetic field conditions is the measure that directly determines the ability of a receiver to power implanted bioelectronics. To demonstrate this, the WPT receiver was driven at magnetic field strengths up to the 205 µTRMS, the whole-body limit of IEEE C95.12019[33], with power delivered to a matched resistive load. 

The optimal load impedance for maximum power transfer was determined from the mBVD circuit model fit to the S21 measurement (Supplementary Note 2). At resonance, the impedances of the motional inductor and capacitor cancel, leaving the motional resistance as the sole impedance in the motional branch. Since the electrical parallel capacitance impedance is much greater than the motional resistance at the 100 kHz resonance, the total device impedance at resonance is approximately equal to the motional resistance alone. The motional resistance of approximately 10 kΩ, determined from the -39.9 dB insertion loss of the S21 measurement (Supplementary Note 3), sets the optimal matched load impedance for maximum power delivery. A 10 kΩ resistor was connected across the output port of the 

WPT receiver to ground, with a high-impedance voltage spectrum analyzer connected in parallel to monitor the voltage drop across the load. A time-varying excitation magnetic field was applied at frequencies swept through the device resonance, with the current through the AC magnetic field coils monitored to determine the applied magnetic field strength. The power delivered by the WPT receiver was calculated from the RMS voltage across the load resistor as P = VRMS[2] / RL. The WPT receiver delivered power to the matched 10 kΩ load across a range of magnetic field strengths spanning below and slightly above the 205 µTRMS wholebody limit of IEEE C95.1[33], reaching an output of 1.03 µW at 207.95 µTRMS and 1.18 µW at the highest tested field strength of 215.6 µTRMS. Scaling the 1.03 µW output power at 207.95 µTRMS to 205 µTRMS by its squared magnetic field relation yields an output power of 1 µW at the IEEE Std C95.1-2019 limit.

## Discussion 

The MEMS ME WPT receiver demonstrated in this work integrates AlScN piezoelectric and Fe50Co50/Ag ML magnetostrictive thin-films in a heterostructure within a total device volume of 6.24 × 10[-4] mm[3] and delivers 1 µW of power to a matched resistive load at the 205 µTRMS whole-body magnetic field limit of IEEE C95.1-2019 at 100 kHz[33], the optimal frequency for ME WPT under human exposure safety constraints. 

The device achieves a FOMP of 4.05 × 10[-3] mW cm[-3] Oe[-2] Hz[-1] , the highest reported among all ME WPT receivers and 20 times greater than the next best device operating within an order of magnitude in frequency[13, 53, 57-60]. Additionally, the power density is the highest of any ME WPT receiver in literature by a factor of more than 50[53, 59], and the ME coupling coe�icient of 1274 V cm[-1] Oe[-1] exceeds that of similarly sized, comparable-frequency ME WPT devices by more than 50%[40, 42]. These records arise from the combination of the enhanced piezoelectric coe�icient of AlScN, the high piezomagnetic coe�icient of the Fe50Co50/Ag ML magnetostrictive, and the high quality factor achievable through MEMS microfabrication. 

limit is su�icient to power a range of reported implanted bioelectronic devices; neural recorders[26] and amplifier circuitry[52], biomolecule sensors[61], and temperature sensors[62] have been demonstrated at power levels within this range. For devices that require more power but operate in the limbs, such as fingertip force sensors[1], higher magnetic field strengths are permitted, up to 37.9 mTRMS at 100 kHz[33]. Devices in the limbs with higher power requirements can benefit both from the higher permissible field levels and the HAC[2] relation of power with magnetic field. Additionally, the WPT receiver presented is highly scalable, with arrays of resonators in series or parallel increasing the power through an increase in output current or voltage respectively. An increase in parallel resonant beams on a single device may also increase the output power more rapidly than the area scaling would suggest. The surface stress COMSOL simulation in Figure 2a shows the resonant beams closest to the tethers experiencing less stress than those at the center. As such, tether losses with additional parallel beams may become a less dominant mechanical loss 

mechanism, resulting in the power output increasing at a faster rate than the area scaling for additional parallel resonant beams. 

The ME WPT receivers demonstrated in this work were tested under 4 mBar vacuum to reduce viscous damping and achieve a high quality factor flexural-mode resonance. Vacuum packaging of the device through thin-film hermetic die-to-die bonding can provide a path toward maintaining this performance in implanted systems[63]. Additionally, a 4 mT magnetic field bias was used to maximize the magnetostriction response of the Fe50Co50/Ag ML film. In an implanted system, the DC bias requirement necessitates permanent magnets or electromagnets. While the receiver can be used at a lower DC magnetic field, as low as no bias field at all, the small-signal magnetostriction response, and thus output power, are impacted by the lower bias field. Previous work has shown that a self-biased ME composite is possible through either an exchange bias e�ect, through particular selection of magnetic and antiferromagnetic materials, or through control of the magnetostrictive material’s thinfilm residual stresses[56]. Through the self-biasing of the magnetostrictive film, an AC magnetic field coil can produce the bias field and AC excitation field, instead of requiring both an AC coil and on-body permanent magnets or a large electromagnet to produce the 

This work demonstrates a sub-millimeter MEMS ME WPT receiver delivering 1 µW at the IEEE C95.1-2019 whole-body magnetic field safety limit and exhibits a record figure of merit and ME coupling coe�icient among comparable-frequency ME WPT devices. Additionally, the power density is the highest reported of ME WPT receivers in literature. The integration of aluminum scandium nitride piezoelectric and iron-cobalt/silver multilayer magnetostrictive thin-films within a microfabricated MEMS heterostructure achieves high magnetoelectric coupling with a high quality factor resonator. Miniaturized magnetoelectric wireless power transfer receivers overcome limitations to sub-millimeter size-scaling that hamper ultrasonic and inductive wireless power modalities and enable the powering of biomedical sensors and systems implanted into anatomically constrained locations, including in the brain, fingertips, and eyes. As implantable bioelectronic devices continue to miniaturize, MEMS magnetoelectric transduction establishes a scalable platform for battery-free wireless power delivery that will allow for the next generation of implantable sensing and stimulation systems.

## Methods 

## Fabrication 

detailed in Supplementary Note 5. Devices were fabricated on a 4-inch diameter intrinsic (100) silicon wafer substrate with resistivity of >10 kΩ-cm. A bottom electrode of 15 nm titanium / 150 nm platinum was sputter deposited (Evatec Clusterline 200 II) to produce (111) oriented Pt. An aqua regia etch was masked with S1813 photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) to etch through the field area of the bottom electrode platinum. The S1813 masking photoresist was stripped with Microposit 1165 remover (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) and oxygen plasma (PIE Scientific Tergeo-Plus Plasma Cleaner). 

A 1 µm thick Al0.67Sc0.33 deposition tool. The AlScN film was grown as a four-layer stack: an AlN seed layer, and AlNto-AlScN gradient layer, and a bilayer of tensile and compressive AlScN films deposited at 30 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm) and 21 sccm N2 respectively, following prior work on stress-neutral AlScN films[69]. A full description of deposition parameters, including powers, deposition times, and target-to-substrate distance are described in Supplementary Note 5, step E. 

Vias through the AlScN to the bottom electrode Pt were formed using a silicon nitride hard mask grown by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (Oxford PlasmaLab 100 PECVD) patterned with S1813 photoresist and etched in a reactive ion etcher (RIE, Oxford 80 Plus RIE). The photoresist was stripped in 1165 remover before a heated potassium hydroxide solution etched through the AlScN. The remaining silicon nitride was stripped with CF4 RIE plasma. 

LOR 10A (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) and S1813 photoresists were spun, exposed, and developed. RIE using CF4 plasma was used to etch through the oxide layer and land on the AlScN. A 10 nm Ti / 100 nm Pt top electrode was sputter deposited (Denton Explorer14 Magnetron Sputterer). The top electrode was lifted o� in 1165 remover, and the remaining silicon dioxide was stripped in CF4 RIE plasma. 

The resonator geometry was created with an etch through the AlScN. A 3 µm silicon dioxide film was deposited by PECVD to act as the etch mask for the AlScN etch. 10 nm Aluminum was deposited above the oxide in the Denton sputterer. S1818 photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) was spun, exposed, and developed, which additionally etched through the 10 nm Al film. The silicon dioxide was etched through to the AlScN using CF4 RIE plasma with the S1818 mask. Any remaining photoresist was stripped in 1165 remover. A 

variable-angle ion mill etch described in step K in Supplementary Note 5 was performed to produce a vertical sidewall on the AlScN. Remaining silicon dioxide was stripped with CHF3/O2 plasma in the RIE. 

The Fe50Co50/Ag magnetostrictive multilayer was patterned and deposited next. LOR 20B (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) and S1813 photoresists were spun, exposed, and developed. Fe50Co50/Ag ML, (10 nm/3 nm)×77, was deposited, with deposition conditions described in step M in Supplementary Note 5. The magnetostrictive film was lifted o� in 1165 remover with the assistance of a permanent magnet. 

The 4-inch wafer was diced into the 2 × 2 mm die (ADT 7100 Dicing Saw) and released in XeF2 gas (SPTS/Xactix). The released die were die-attached to a breakout PCB with epoxy and wire bonded (Kulicke & So�a Wire Bonder). Through-hole SMA PCB adapters were soldered to the PCB.

A full fabrication flow is described below, with drawings of the cross section at each step shown in Supplementary Figure 5. 

A) A 4-inch diameter intrinsic (100) silicon wafer substrate with resistivity of >10 kΩ-cm was used for device fabrication. 

B) Blanket 15 nm titanium and 150 nm platinum were sputtered to produce (111) oriented Pt (Evatec Clusterline 200 II). The chuck temperature was 500˚C. Ti was sputtered with DC power (1 kW) for 14 seconds, with a target-to-substrate distance of 101 mm and 45 sccm of argon gas flow into the chamber during deposition. After the Ti deposition, the Pt was DC sputtered (850 W) for 60 seconds, with a target-to-substrate distance of -91 mm and 40 sccm of argon gas flow into the chamber during deposition. 

C) S1813 photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) was used to mask the platinum etch. The photoresist was exposed with 90 mJ/cm[2] i-line light (SUSS MicroTec MA6 Gen3 Mask Aligner). MF CD-26 Developer (Microposit) was used for the development of the S1813 photoresist. Unless stated otherwise, all future photoresist exposures and developments use the SUSS MicroTec MA6 and CD-26 developer, respectively. 

D) An aqua regia solution of HCl and HNO3 in a volume ratio of 1:4 at 60 ˚C was used to etch the bottom electrode platinum. The S1813 masking photoresist was stripped with Microposit 1165 remover (Kayaku Advanced Materials inc.) and oxygen plasma (PIE Scientific Tergeo-Plus Plasma Cleaner). All photoresist removals use 1165 remover unless stated otherwise. 

E) A 1 µm thick aluminum scandium nitride (Al0.67Sc0.33N) film was pulsed-DC sputtered in the same Evatec sputter deposition tool. The AlScN thin-film was deposited as four layers: an aluminum nitride (AlN) seed layer, AlN to AlScN gradient, an AlScN film deposited under high gas flow, and an AlScN film deposited under low gas flow, following prior work growing stress-neutral and stress-gradient neutral AlScN films[4]. The AlN seed and gradient provide a gradual alloying of scandium into AlN, and the bilayer AlScN films, controlled by N2 gas flow, allow for an overall stress-neutral and stress-gradient-neutral piezoelectric film stack 

For AlScN deposition, the target-to-substrate distance was set to 104 mm, with the chuck temperature at 450 ˚C. An 86 second aluminum nitride seed layer was deposited at 30 sccm N2 gas flow and 1000 W applied to the 100 mm diameter Al target for a 15 nm thickness. For all depositions described for the AlScN stack, the chopper frequency of the pulsed DC sputtering was 150 kHz, with a 800 ns chopper pulse off time. A gradient layer from AlN to AlScN was co-sputtered after the AlN seed layer. The power on the 100 mm diameter scandium target ramped linearly from 0 W to 655 W over the duration of 162 

seconds, with the power on the Al target at 1 kW and N2 gas flow at 30 sccm. Once the power on the Sc target reached 655 W, the deposition was continued at the same conditions for an additional 1979 seconds. The 1000/655 W ratio of powers applied to the Al/Sc targets produced a AlScN film with scandium concentration of approximately 33%. After the total 2141 seconds of gradient and AlScN layers was completed at 30 sccm, the N2 gas flow was dropped to 21 sccm, and the deposition was continued at the lower gas flow with the, otherwise, same process conditions for 1980 seconds. The total 4207 seconds of deposition produced a 1 µm AlScN thin-film. 

F) Vias were formed through the AlScN to form an electrical contact to the bottom electrode Pt. Non-stoichiometric silicon nitride (SiNx) was grown by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (Oxford PlasmaLab 100 PECVD), patterned with S1813 photoresist, and etched with CF4 plasma in a reactive ion etcher (RIE) (Oxford 80 Plus RIE). The photoresist was stripped in 1165 remover. 

G) The wafer was submersed in 45 ˚C heated potassium hydroxide (KOH) for about 10 minutes, and vias through the AlScN were etched, masked by the SiNx. The SiNx mask was stripped with CF4 RIE. 

H) To create the top electrode Pt, a 143 nm silicon dioxide (SiO2) layer was grown with PECVD, with a 650 nm LOR 10A (Kayaku Advanced Materials Inc.) and 1.4 µm S1813 spun above the SiO2 to mask the negative of the top electrode area. The SiO2 was etched through with CHF3 and O2 plasma in the RIE. 

I) A 10 nm Ti adhesion layer and 100 nm top electrode platinum was sputter deposited (Denton Explorer14 Magnetron Sputterer). The top electrode Pt was lifted off in 1165 remover, and the remaining SiO2 was stripped in CF4 plasma. 

J) A 3 µm thick SiO2 mask layer was deposited using PECVD to create a hard mask for AlScN etching. 10 nm of aluminum was sputter deposited above the SiO2 mask (Denton) to provide high RIE etch selectivity. S1818 photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials inc.) was spun and patterned. The development of the S1818 photoresist with MF CD-26 Developer (Microposit) additionally etched the 10nm Al layer at the patterned region. The SiO2 mask was etched completely through with CF4 plasma in the RIE. Any remaining photoresist was stripped in 1165 remover. 

K) Ion milling through the AlScN was completed using a variable angle etch with accelerating voltage of 500 V. The variable angle etch included a 30 second etch at 10˚ angle, where a 0˚ angle equates to the wafer plane being normal to the direction of the ion beam, followed by etching during a 3.7˚/second rotation to 70˚, and an etch at 70˚ for 15 seconds. This variable-angle 1 minute etch cycle results in a steep sidewall etch of AlScN, 

with an AlScN etch rate of approximately 30 nm/minute. The wafer was cooled for 1 minute, and the etch and cooldown cycles were repeated for 40 cycles, resulting in over-etch into the silicon for XeF2 release. After the etch completed, the remaining SiO2 was stripped with CHF3/O2 RIE. 

L) To pattern the magnetostrictive FeCo/Ag ML, LOR 20B (Kayaku Advanced Materials inc.) and S1813 were spun on the wafer and patterned. 

M) The 1 µm FeCo/Ag ML was sputter deposited as a 77 multilayer of 10nm Fe0.5Co0.5 separated by 3 nm Ag (AJA Internation Inc. Orion). The Ag target was mounted in an unbalanced configuration, and the Fe0.5Co0.5 target was mounted in a flux concentrator configuration. The FeCo was deposited with pulsed DC power (100W / 100 kHz, 2 µs), and the Ag was deposited with 50 W RF power. Argon gas was flowed into the system at a rate of 30 sccm, with the chamber pressure held at 3 mTorr during deposition. A DC voltage bias was applied to the sample substrate holder of -95 V during deposition, yielding a nearly stress neutral film (0 +/- 20 MPa). The FeCo/Ag ML was capped with 20 nm of Pt before venting the chamber to prevent oxidation of the magnetic material. After deposition, the FeCo/Ag ML was lifted off in 1165 Remover with the assistance of a permanent magnet hovered over the wafer.

paper.title: SMILE: A Structured Multi-Agent Clinical Reasoning for Liver Ultrasound Understanding
paper.abstract: Automated liver ultrasound report generation improves the diagnosis of liver diseases by producing clinically structured descriptions of anatomical and disease-related findings. However, current generative vision-language models (VLMs) often rely on a single reasoning pathway that maps ultrasound appearance directly to textual descriptions. In addition to the inherent vision-language modality gap, this design is limited for liver ultrasound because disease interpretation is constrained by subtle visual evidence, heterogeneous disease patterns, and limited paired supervision. To address these limitations, we propose SMILE, a Structured Multi-agent clInicaL rEasoning framework that uses multiple complementary specialist agents to interpret ultrasound images and consolidates their outputs through a judge-guided consensus mechanism. Our approach employs three specialized agents: an image interpretation agent for morphological descriptions, a clinical-stage reasoning agent, and a visual question answering (VQA) agent for targeted queries. These agent responses are then aggregated and scrutinized by a judge VLM using a consensus filtering prompt to produce a unified, clinically coherent output. Across a public liver ultrasound dataset and an internal clinical dataset, SMILE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLMs, achieving up to 19.0\% improvement in ROUGE-1 and 18.8\% improvement in clinical F1-score, while reaching VQA F1-scores of 0.82 and 0.65 on public and internal datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of SMILE for data-scarce and limited-supervision clinical settings. Our models, datasets, and code are available \href{https://github.com/CMME-Lab/SMILE}{here}.

paper.title: Fundamental Limits and Joint Design for Monostatic Joint Communications and Sensing in LEO Satellites
paper.abstract: Monostatic joint communication and sensing (JCAS) from a low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite requires full-duplex (FD) operation, with self-interference (SI) $80$--$100$~dB stronger than the ground echo. The echo returns milliseconds after transmission, whereas the onboard coupling spans a few symbols. We develop a theory and a design that exploit this separation. Restricting the analog and digital cancellers to the short SI support is without loss of optimality and essential in practice: a least-squares canceller whose support contains the target delay absorbs the coherent echo and reduces the radar SINR by a closed-form factor, about $18$~dB for a vessel at its zero-Doppler crossing. Modeling the SI that no linear canceller can reconstruct as spatially white and accounting for ADC quantization, we derive in closed form a ceiling on the radar SINR, the minimum pre-ADC SI power under a canceller tap budget, the budget for full cancellation, and the sensing weight at which the optimal design changes over from communication to sensing. We then maximize a weighted sum of the communication and sensing SINRs, each normalized by its half-duplex benchmark, over the beamformers, sensing covariance, combiners, and cancellers for $K$ users and $Q$ targets, using an alternating algorithm with closed-form updates. Simulations confirm the closed forms. The joint design gains up to $13\%$ in the normalized objective over a sequential design that cancels the SI only at the receiver, and more than $10$~dB of downlink and radar SINR with $4$-bit ADCs and in the 10th-percentile worst-target SINR of four targets, whereas ignoring the SI overloads the ADCs.

paper.title: Harnessing Inter-Waveguide Evanescent Coupling in Pinching-Antenna Systems
paper.abstract: In multi-waveguide pinching-antenna systems (PASS), waveguides are typically modeled as independent signal-transport paths. However, when dielectric waveguides are closely spaced, their evanescent electromagnetic fields overlap, allowing guided signals to exchange energy before radiation. While such inter-waveguide coupling is conventionally regarded as undesirable crosstalk, this paper reveals an opportunity to harness it as an additional analog beamforming resource. The key insight is that coupling, through its interaction with sequential signal extraction by distributed pinching antennas (PAs), can reshape coherent signal combining at the receivers without increasing the available signal power. Consequently, stronger coupling does not necessarily yield better performance; rather, the coupling-induced phase relationships determine whether the radiated signals combine constructively or destructively. To characterize and exploit this mechanism, we establish a physics-based end-to-end channel model, derive coupling-aware waveguide-spacing principles and achievable-rate bounds, and develop joint waveguide deployment, PA placement, and digital precoding algorithms for multi-hotspot communications. Numerical results demonstrate substantial sum-rate improvements over conventional fixed-deployment and optimized minimum-spacing PASS benchmarks. These findings establish inter-waveguide evanescent coupling as a new physical degree of freedom for PASS channel reconfiguration.

paper.title: Direct Covariance-to-Beamformer Mapping for Low-Latency Hybrid ISAC Beamforming with Subsequent DoA Estimation
paper.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems typically employ a two-stage beamforming pipeline, in which target directions are first estimated from the received covariance matrix and then used to compute the beamforming weights by solving non-convex optimization problems. Although effective, this approach introduces processing latency that can limit beam adaptation in dynamic environments. This letter proposes a beamforming deep neural network (BFDNN) for direct covariance-to-beamformer learning in ISAC systems. BFDNN is a compact regression network that maps covariance-matrix features directly to the hybrid beamforming weights produced by a hybrid ISAC beamformer, eliminating the direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation stage during inference. Compared with MUSIC, classification-DNN, and regression-DNN based beamforming pipelines, BFDNN generates comparable beam patterns and higher effective spectral efficiencies while reducing the beamforming prediction latency by 25-30 times on the evaluated platform, demonstrating the potential of direct covariance-to-beamformer learning for low-latency ISAC beam updates. Moreover, the target directions can be inferred indirectly from the generated radiation pattern, yielding DoA accuracy competitive with that of dedicated learning-based methods in the evaluated scenario.

paper.title: Energy-Efficient Tri-Hybrid Beamforming with Movable Pattern-Reconfigurable Antennas
paper.abstract: Conventional hybrid precoding is confined to the digital/analog domains, leaving the spatial and radiation-pattern degrees-of-freedoms (DoFs) largely untapped. To unlock these, we propose a movable pattern-reconfigurable antenna (MPRA) and an energy-efficient tri-hybrid framework that jointly optimizes the precoders, antenna positions, and radiation-pattern states. We develop a hardware-inspired power model capturing the energy and transmission-time costs of antenna reconfiguration. The resulting mixed discrete-continuous fractional problem is solved via an alternating-optimization framework combining fractional programming, Riemannian optimization, and switching-aware pattern optimization. Simulations demonstrate near-exhaustive-search performance and consistent energy-efficiency (EE) gains, validating the complementary benefits of antenna movement, pattern reconfiguration, and tri-hybrid precoding under hardware-inspired power and latency costs.

paper.title: Movable-Element Multi-Functional RIS-Assisted Hybrid RSMA-NOMA: A Constrained Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Approach
paper.abstract: In this work, we propose a movable-element (ME) multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface (MF-RIS) architecture, termed MM-RIS, which integrates element mobility with adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and energy harvesting (EH) to enhance communication flexibility and energy self-sustainability. A hybrid rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) transmission scheme is further designed to improve spectral efficiency. We formulate an energy efficiency (EE) maximization problem by jointly optimizing transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS configurations, panel deployment, and ME positions. To address the resulting non-convex mixed continuous-discrete optimization problem, we propose constrained hybrid deep reinforcement learning with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS). CRAFTS integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-networks (MADQN) through bi-directional parametrized sharing to handle continuous and discrete actions, respectively. Moreover, a transformer-based architecture and federated learning (FL) are incorporated to enhance state representation and distributed knowledge sharing, whilst a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism facilitates the constraint satisfaction. Simulation results have demonstrated that the proposed MM-RIS architecture and CRAFTS framework substantially improve EE and constraint satisfaction compared to the benchmarks in the open literature. Moreover, the results validate the benefits of spatially reconfigurable MM-RIS, hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions, and intelligent collaborative learning, highlighting the potential of the proposed framework for energy-efficient and adaptive next-generation wireless networks.

\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Background and Literature Reviews}
In the era of sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications, the scarcity of spectrum resources and the explosive growth in heterogeneous service demands have driven researchers to explore more efficient and flexible transmission technologies \cite{1}. To further enhance spectral and interference management in dense wireless deployments, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) has recently emerged as a highly promising transmission strategy \cite{2}. By splitting messages into common and private components and superimposing them through linear precoding, RSMA provides flexible interference handling. Owing to this flexibility, RSMA demonstrates improved robustness against imperfect channel state information and offers superior rate-reliability trade-offs in interference-limited environments \cite{3}. However, despite its advantages, the performance of RSMA may still be insufficient in highly dynamic or heavily loaded networks, where interference suppression remains challenging. To further maximize its performance potential, successive interference cancellation (SIC) from non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) \cite{noma} can be incorporated into RSMA, forming a hybrid structure. By combining rate-splitting capability of RSMA with power-domain multiplexing of NOMA \cite{7}, such hybrid design enhances multi-user signal separation and strengthens interference mitigation, enabling greater spectral efficiency and improved link reliability. However, the performance of such multiple accesses is often hindered by severe channel fading and inter-user interference, which potentially degrades the signal quality and limits its practical deployment \cite{9}. 
To address the above-mentioned issues, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have been proposed as an enabling technology \cite{10, 11}. By adjusting the configuration of RIS elements, a virtual line-of-sight (LoS) link can be established to bypass obstacles between the transmitter and receiver and to improve the signal quality for combating the channel fading \cite{my_fdris3, 12}. Benefited from these advantages, RIS can enable precise signal distribution, significantly improving communication performances. Although RIS holds promise for next-generation wireless networks, its practical deployment remains constrained by several inherent limitations. Specifically, it can only be operated over a 180-degree half-space coverage area, and mainly depends on external power supplies, which confines its independent operation and scalability. To overcome the backdrops, the concept of multi-functional RIS (MF-RIS) has been introduced in \cite{14, my_ojcom}, integrating simultaneous transmission and reflection (STAR) capabilities to provide 360-degree full-space coverage and ubiquitous connectivity \cite{15, 16, my_star}. Additionally, MF-RIS is equipped with radio-frequency (RF) and energy harvesting (EH) circuits, enabling it to capture energy from incident electromagnetic signals and is capable of operating in a self-sustainable manner \cite{18, 19, 20}. Such design alleviates the dependence on wired power infrastructure or frequent battery replacement, enhancing the overall energy efficiency (EE). Furthermore, by embedding active components, MF-RIS is capable of conducting signal amplification \cite{22} for compensating severe path loss, improving the quality-of-services (QoS) of users in weak channel conditions. When combined with advanced multiple access schemes, MF-RIS can substantially strengthen the propagation conditions for user clusters, especially under NOMA-/RSMA-based transmissions. 
However, the practical implementation of active MF-RIS is also hindered by hardware-induced constraints such as the coupled phase-shift effects \cite{23}. Unlike ideal models, active components frequently exhibit a strong interdependence between the phase-shift and amplification gains \cite{24}. This coupling effect might reduce the available DoFs in the optimization space, which necessitates more complex coordination strategies to achieve the desired beamforming gains. To overcome these limitations, beyond static metasurfaces, fluid antenna (FA) systems have recently attracted attention for their ability to dynamically reconfigure the effective antenna position within a given aperture by leveraging fluid-based elements \cite{my_lim, 26}. Similar to FA, movable-antenna (MA) structures \cite{MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4} are also developed. By allowing the radiating point to move within a predefined region, FA/MA can exploit spatial diversity in small-scale fading without requiring multiple RF chains, offering new degrees of freedom (DoFs) at the physical layer. This dynamic ability is particularly appealing in environments with rapidly varying channels or strong blockage effects. In the works of \cite{new1, new2}, antenna position of the MA is deployed to increase the spatial DoF and enhance the performance of the integrated sensing and communication systems. The paper \cite{new3} investigates that the MA is capable of achieving full array gain over the desired direction, whereas null steering in undesired directions can be realized. The work of \cite{new4} further discusses near-field digital and analog beamforming in MA-aided multiuser communication systems. In the work of \cite{6dma}, six-dimensional MA is introduced that exploits the transceiver spatial variation by considering both xyz-positions and rotations to improve performance in terms of geometric array gains, spatial multiplexing and interference mitigation. Inspired by the FA/MA \cite{fas1, 10, MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4}, the movable-elements (ME) are introduced \cite{25, lim1, pat, movele1} to enable element-wise spatial adjustment across three-dimensional (3D) Cartesian axes of xyz-domain. Different from MAs, ME-enhanced RIS further aligning to proper small-scale channels induces a more challenging task when configuring well-positioned elements in the cascaded channels from the base station (BS), RIS to users \cite{lim1}. The authors in \cite{26} have proposed a movable-element RIS (ME-RIS) framework, utilizing an element-wise position optimization approach to significantly enhance beamforming gains. Furthermore, the concept of fluid-element STAR surfaces called FIRES is designed in \cite{27}, which extends the FA capability to STAR-RIS architectures. In paper \cite{new5}, MA-aided NOMA is considered for multi-user downlink communications, where the MA positions at the users, BS beamforming, and SIC decoding indicators are jointly optimized. Moreover, the work of \cite{new6} investigates the benefits of FA with dynamic port reconfiguration for enhancing RSMA performance, where the outage probability and ergodic rate are analyzed to quantify the performance gains provided by FA. However, most existing FA/MA-integrated works focus on single-link scenarios or basic reflection/transmission structures, relying on the external power grid usage. The integration of ME into MF-RISs that simultaneously supports element mobility, reflection/transmission capability, signal amplification, and self-sustainable EH remains largely unexplored. 
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), the integration of learning-based optimizations into wireless communication systems has become an important research trend \cite{11, 29}, especially for complex environments. Owing to the strong coupling between multiple strategies such as beamforming and RIS configurations, the resulting optimization problems typically exhibit high dimensionality, non-linearity, and mixed discrete-continuous structures, rendering traditional analytical or convex-approximation methods inadequate in highly dynamic environments. In addressing these challenges, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely adopted for resource allocation and control \cite{11, my_rl_wu, 30, han, 31, my_rl_yt} thanks to its capability of learning near-optimal policies from interactions with complex environments. In DRL, an agent performs the determined actions and then attains rewards, followed by the observed updated states for the next-round policy decision. In \cite{11}, a multi-agent system is considered, where each agent corresponds to an individual RIS, and the joint beamforming and RIS deployment are optimized using multi-agent RL techniques. In paper \cite{29}, a multi-agent system is designed for low-complexity beamforming and power control in multi-antenna-based NOMA networks. The work of \cite{my_rl_wu} designs a hierarchical RL structure for RIS optimizations, where the core-RL optimizes the beamforming and configurations, whereas auxiliary RL optimizes the hyperparameters of core-RL for better learning process. Nonetheless, most existing DRL approaches are either centralized, leading to scalability and overhead issues, or designed for purely continuous or purely discrete state-action spaces, which are inadequate for complex wireless networks. This motivates the development of hybrid DRL frameworks that can handle continuous-discrete action spaces in a unified manner \cite{30, han, 31, my_ojcom}. In the work of \cite{30}, hybrid continuous and discrete action outputs are designed as a parametrized sharing architecture. Extended from \cite{30}, the paper \cite{han} designs hybrid DRL for tackling continuous STAR-RIS configurations and the discrete coupled-phase problems. The work of \cite{31} designs twin-models and bi-directional sharing structure in hybrid DRL architecture for complex MF-RIS policies associated with continuous-discrete actions. 
Furthermore, conventional DRL architectures relying solely on multiple deep neural layer learning may struggle to capture complex dependencies between high-dimensional states and actions, especially in multi-agent coordination. To address this, adoption of transformer architectures \cite{32, my_ojcom} for enhancing feature extraction and representation learning is needed \cite{my_ojcom, 33}. Additionally, federated learning (FL) \cite{34} is utilized for enabling decentralized model aggregation and privacy-aware knowledge sharing across distributed learning agents without raw data exchange. In addition to architectural enhancements, ensuring strict adherence to operational boundaries such as QoS and power limits is crucial for practical reliability. While conventional reward shaping is often used to penalize constraint violations, its static nature frequently fails to maintain an optimal balance between performance optimization and safety requirements \cite{35, 37}. This necessitates the adoption of Lagrangian-based primal-dual optimization techniques \cite{35}, i.e., an adaptive Lagrangian multiplier method to dynamically tune penalty coefficients based on instantaneous violations. However, the applications of enhanced architectures of multi-agent hybrid DRL with transformer, parametrized sharing, federated cooperation, and adaptive Lagrangian constraint management to complex wireless network systems remain substantially unexplored. \subsection{Challenges and Contributions}
The integration of ME and MF-RIS with hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions remains unstudied but introduces several fundamental challenges. The incorporation of MEs into MF-RIS significantly enlarges the spatial DoFs, leading to a high-dimensional and highly-coupled optimization problem involving beamforming, power control, rate allocation, phase-shift coefficients, and metasurface locations as well as element positions. The comparable overhead associated with ME, including movement power consumption and repositioning delay may be introduced and cannot be neglected compared to the operational power and channel coherence time. This results in a non-convex mixed continuous-discrete problem that is difficult to solve using conventional optimization techniques. Additionally, the hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmission scheme introduces complex interference structures across clustered users, which require dynamic and coordinated resource allocation to strike a compelling balance between spectral efficiency and interference mitigation. The coupling transmissions among communication variables further increases the difficulty of joint optimization. Furthermore, the presence of EH and amplification functionalities imposes stringent system constraints of power budgets, QoS requirements, and hardware limitations. Self-sustainable capability should be achieved while supporting multiple functionalities of MF-RIS. From algorithmic perspectives, the large-scale multi-agent nature of complex wireless networks leads to scalability and non-stationarity issues, where centralized learning becomes impractical due to excessive overhead, whilst decentralized learning suffers from limited coordination and potential convergence issues. This motivates us to conceive an advanced DRL-based framework for the integration of ME and MF-RIS in hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions. The main contributions of this paper are elaborated as follows:
\begin{itemize}
	\item We propose a novel ME-enhanced MF-RIS (MM-RIS)-assisted communication framework for hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmissions. The proposed MM-RIS integrates MEs with a deployable MF-RIS capabilities, enabling adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and EH, which significantly enhances system adaptability, coverage, and energy self-sustainability in dynamic wireless environments.
	\item We formulate an EE maximization problem for the proposed MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA. The problem jointly optimizes transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS parameters of amplitude coefficients, phase-shifts, and EH ratios, as well as metasurface deployment and ME positions. The formulated problem is highly non-convex and involves mixed continuous-discrete variables with intricate coupling constraints under practical limitations such as BS power budgets, user rate requirements and rate allocation bounds as well as minimum inter-element spacing, coupled phase-shifts, self-sustainability, and deployment boundaries of MM-RIS.
	\item We develop a constrained hybrid reinforcement learning framework with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS) scheme which integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-network (MADQN) to handle continuous and discrete decision variables, respectively. A transformer-based architecture is incorporated to capture complex state-action dependencies, while FL is employed to facilitate decentralized training and accelerate convergence via collaborative knowledge sharing. Moreover, a bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism is proposed to enable coordinated optimization across heterogeneous action spaces. Furthermore, to guarantee constraint satisfaction, a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism is conceived to dynamically update multipliers, ensuring stable and reliable learning under practical system constraints.
	\item Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CRAFTS-enabled MM-RIS framework significantly outperforms the conventional benchmarks, including standalone PPO/DQN, non-coupled learning benchmarks, and different single-functional RIS architectures without amplification or EH in the open literature. Particularly, the proposed MM-RIS-aided RSMA-NOMA achieves substantial EE gains and constraint satisfaction across diverse scenarios, validating the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed architecture for next-generation wireless networks.
\end{itemize}

Section \ref{sec_alg} elaborates the proposed framework of CRAFTS. Simulation results are provided in Section \ref{sec_sim}, whereas the conclusion is drawn in Section \ref{sec_con}.

\subsection{Channel Model}
We consider the Rician fading channel model \cite{31} between the BS and the $q$-th MM-RIS as $\mathbf{H}_{q} \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N}$
\begin{align}
	\mathbf{H}_q = \sqrt{h_0 d_{q}^{-k_0}}
\left( \sqrt{\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}} \right),
\label{4}
\end{align}
where $h_0$ is the pathloss at the reference distance of 1 meter, $d_{q}= \|\mathbf{w}_b-\mathbf{w}_q\| $ is the distance between BS and MM-RIS $q$, and $k_0$ is the pathloss exponent. Notation of $\beta_0$ represents the Rician factor adjusting the portion of LoS path $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}}$ and non-LoS (NLoS) component of $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$. The LoS component $ \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} $ is expressed as \cite{26} $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}'_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q) \mathbf{a}_b^{\mathrm{H}}(\psi_b)$,
where $(\cdot)^{\mathrm{H}}$ indicates the Hermitian operation. The transmit steering vector of the BS and the receiving steering vector of the $q$-th MM-RIS associated with the $m$-th ME are respectively given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align}
	[\mathbf{a}_b(\psi_b)]_n &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (n-1) \sin(\psi_b)}, 
	[\mathbf{a}_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{a,q} \cos\psi'_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{e,q}\right)},
 \label{6}
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $[ \cdot ]_n$ represents the $n$-th entry of the vector. Notation of $\lambda$ indicates the wavelength, whilst $\psi_b$ denotes the angle-of-departure (AoD) from the BS towards MM-RIS. Symbols of $\psi'_{a,q}$ and $\psi'_{e,q}$ denote the azimuth and elevation angles-of-arrival (AoAs) at MM-RIS $q$, respectively. Following \eqref{4}, the channel between the $q$-th MM-RIS and user $U_{kj}$ is defined as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj} \in \mathbb{C}^{M\times 1}$, where the distance between them is denoted as $d_{q, kj} = \| \mathbf{w}_q - \mathbf{w}_{kj} \|$. The LoS channel of $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}$ can be expressed as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)$,
where $\psi''_{a,q}$ and $\psi''_{e,q}$ respectively denote the azimuth and elevation AoDs from the MM-RIS towards user $U_{kj}$, and the corresponding elementwise steering vector is defined as
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  = e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{a,q} \cos\psi''_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{e,q}\right)}.
 \label{eq:fires_user_channel}
\end{align}
As for the NLoS components related to MM-RIS-based channel, i.e., $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}}$, Jake's model is adopted to model the ME-induced spatial correlation \cite{my_lim}, i.e., $[\mathbf{J}_{q}]_{i,j} = J_0 \left( \frac{2\pi \Delta d_{i,j}}{\lambda} \right)$, where $J_0$ is the Bessel function of the zero order and $\Delta d_{i,j}$ denotes the distances between the $i$-th and the $j$-th MM-RIS elements. where $\bar{\mathbf{H}}_q$ and $\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{q,kj}$ represent the uncorrelated small-scale fading components, which are modeled as complex Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. \subsection{Signal Model}
In the hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmission, users are first partitioned into multiple groups to efficiently share the limited spectrum resources. Specifically, a channel-aware user grouping procedure is performed prior to resource optimization. Users are first classified according to whether they are located on the reflection or transmission side of the MM-RIS. Users on each side are then further partitioned into multiple groups according to their effective channel directions. For users $u$ and $v$, their channel correlation is defined as $\rho_{u,v} = \frac{ |\mathbf g_u\mathbf g_v^{\rm H}| }{ \|\mathbf g_u\|_2\|\mathbf g_v\|_2 }$. Users exhibiting high channel correlation are preferentially assigned to the same group to facilitate beamforming. In each group at direction $k$, data stream is split into common and private streams. The common stream decodes messages for all users, whereas the private stream provides individual data content to each user. Moreover, in private message, NOMA mechanism is employed to further superimpose private signals for enhancing the frequency utilizations. Therefore, the BS transmits signals containing the common stream $s_k^c$ and the private stream $s_{kj}$ for user $U_{kj}$. The signal received by user $U_{kj}$ can be given by

During the repositioning of the MEs, the channel undergoes rapid time-varying fluctuations, potentially resulting in severe degradation of the received signal quality. Accordingly, each transmission block of duration $T$ is partitioned into two phases, namely the ME movement phase and the communication phase. Specifically, the MM-RIS panel positions are slow-timescale variables that are updated according to relatively slowly varying network conditions, such as user spatial distributions and large scale channel characteristics. In contrast, the MEs are locally repositioned within the surface region on a comparatively faster timescale to adapt to spatial channel variations. Accordingly, the movement-overhead term in the considered EE model accounts for the element-level ME reconfiguration, whereas the transient movement energy and delay associated with relocating an entire MM-RIS panel are not included in each communication optimization cycle.
To elaborate a little further, the proposed MM-RIS architecture can be extended to a general MIMO scenario where each user is equipped with multiple receive antennas. In this case, the equivalent effective channel between the BS and users will be generalized to a matrix-based channel, and additional receive beamforming should be introduced at users. Accordingly, the received signal and SINR can be reformulated by incorporating the receive beamforming, whilst the MM-RIS configurations remain applicable. The corresponding receive beamforming variables can be incorporated into the continuous action space of the proposed learning framework.
\subsection{EH and Power Consumption Model}
Here, we define the EH coefficient matrix for the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS as $\mathbf{T}_{q,m}=\operatorname{diag} \left( \left[ {0, \dots, 0}, 
1 - \alpha_{q,m}, {0, \dots, 0}\right] \right)$. Therefore, the RF power received by the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS is given by $P_{q,m}^{\text{RF}}=\mathbb{E} \left( \left\| \mathbf{T}_{q,m} \left( \mathbf{H}_{q} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\mathbf{f}_k^c + \mathbf{f}_k^p)+ \mathbf{n}_{q,m} \right) \right\|^2 \right)$, where $\mathbf{n}_{q,m}$ is the amplified noise introduced by the MM-RIS hardware with power $\sigma_s^2$. To capture the dynamics of the RF energy conversion efficiency for different input power levels, a nonlinear EH model is adopted \cite{14, 31}. Accordingly, the total harvested power of the $m$-th element of the $q$-th MM-RIS is expressed as $P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}} = \frac{\Upsilon_{q,m} - Z\Omega}{1 - \Omega}$, where $\Upsilon_{q,m}=Z / (1 + e^{-\varrho_1 \left( P_{q,m}^{\text{RF}} - \varrho_2 \right)} )$ is a logistic function, and $Z>0$ is a constant determining
the maximum harvested power. Constant $\Omega=\frac{1}{1+e^{\varrho_1 \varrho_2}}$ ensures a zero-input/zero-output response in H mode in conjucation with constants $\varrho_1>0$ and $\varrho_2 > 0$ capturing the joint effects of circuit sensitivity limitations and current leakage. 
 Moreover, the power for controlling the MM-RIS comes from the total number of PIN diodes required for the quantization levels \cite{37n38} of EH ratio, amplitude and phase-shifts defined as $L_{\alpha}$, $L_{\beta}$, and $L_{\theta}$, respectively. Accordingly, the total number of PIN diodes required is given by $\log_2 L_{\alpha} + \log_2 L_{\beta} + 2 \log_2 L_{\theta}$. The effective total power consumption of the $q$-th MM-RIS considers the ME moving stage and communication stage, which is represented by
