\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{power1}
	P_{q}^{\text{con}}& = 
	\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \cdot \sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}} v_{q,m} E_{q}^{\text{mov}}
	 + 
	\left(1-\frac{T_{\text{mov}}}{T} \right) \cdot  \left[ \frac{1}{2} \left( \log_{2} L_{\alpha} \right. \right. \notag 
		& \left. \left. + \log_{2} L_{\beta} + 2\log_{2} L_{\theta} \right) \cdot M \cdot P_{\text{pin}} + P_{C} + \xi P_{O,q} \right],
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $P_C$ denotes the power consumed by the RF-to-DC power conversion circuit, and $P_{\text{pin}}$ represents the power consumption per PIN diode. Additionally, $E_{q}^{\text{mov}}$ represents the energy consumption per unit distance due to the movement of MEs. Notation of $\xi$ is the inverse of the amplifier efficiency. The output power of the MM-RIS is given by $P_{O,q} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \sum_{k' \in \mathcal{K}} \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_q^k \mathbf{H}_q (\mathbf{f}_{k'}^c + \mathbf{f}_{k'}^p) \|^2 + \sigma_s^2 \|\boldsymbol{\Theta}_q^k\|_F^2 \right)$, where $\|\cdot\|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm. In order to achieve the self-sustainability of each MM-RIS, the total power consumed should not exceed the harvested power by elements, given by $P_{q}^{\text{con}} \leq \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}$. Therefore, the total power consumption is
\begin{align} \label{power2}
	 P_{\text{tot}} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} (\|\mathbf{f}_{k}^c \|^2 \!+\! \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) + \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}} \left( P^{\text{con}}_q \!-\! \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}} \right),
\end{align}
where the first term indicates the BS beamforming power.
\subsection{Problem Formulation}
The objective is to maximize the system EE while guaranteeing the constraints of minimum user rate requirement, MM-RIS configurations and self-sustainability as well as the operational power limitation, which is formulated as follows:
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{subequations} \label{prob}
 \begin{align}
 &\max_{\substack{\mathbf{f}_{k}^c, \mathbf{f}_{k}^p, p_{k}^c, p_{kj}, R_{kj}^c, 
 \alpha_{q,m}, \beta_{q,m}^k, \theta_{q,m}^k, \mathbf{w}_q,  \mathbf{r}_{q,m}}}
 \quad \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} \frac{R_{kj}}{P_{\text{tot}}} \label{prob_25a} [4pt]
 \text{s.t.} \quad 
 & \eqref{coupl}, \eqref{con_SIC}, \notag 
 & \mathbf{\Theta}_q \in \mathcal{R}_{\mathbf{\Theta}}, \qquad\forall q \in \mathcal{Q}, \label{prob_25b} [2pt]
 &R_{kj} \geq R^{\text{min}}_{kj}, \qquad \forall j \in \mathcal{J},\, \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25c} 
 & P_{q}^{\text{con}} \leq \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}, \qquad\qquad \forall q \in \mathcal{Q},  \label{prob_25d} 
 &\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\| \mathbf{f}_k^c \|^2+ \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) \leq P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}, \label{prob_25e} 
 &p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} = 1, \qquad\ \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25f} 
 & \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} R_{kj}^c \leq \min_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} C_{kj}, \qquad\ \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \label{prob_25g} [2pt]
 &\|\mathbf{r}_{q,m} - \mathbf{r}_{q,m'}\| \geq D, \quad \forall m \neq m', \forall m,m'\in\mathcal{M}, \forall q \in \mathcal{Q}, \label{prob_25h}
 &\mathbf{w}_q \in \mathcal{W}, \qquad \forall q \in \mathcal{Q}. \label{prob_25i}
 \end{align}
\end{subequations}
\endgroup
Constraints \eqref{prob_25b} defines the constraint set of MM-RIS coefficients as $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbf{\Theta}}= \{ \alpha_{q,m} \in \{0,1\}, \beta^k_{q,m} \in [0, \beta^k_{\text{max}}], \theta_{q,m}^k \in [0, 2\pi) | \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}, k\in\mathcal{K}, m\in\mathcal{M} \}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25c} guarantees the minimum rate requirement of each user as $R_{kj}^{\text{min}}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25d} ensures the self-sustainability of MM-RIS, i.e., power consumption of the MM-RIS cannot exceed its harvested power. Constraint \eqref{prob_25e} guarantees that transmit power should be smaller than $P^{\text{max}}_{\text{BS}}$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25f} and \eqref{prob_25g} represent the hybrid NOMA-RSMA power allocation factor and rate allocation limitation, respectively. Constraint \eqref{prob_25h} ensures that the distance between two MEs must be greater than the minimum inter-element spacing $D$. Constraint \eqref{prob_25i} defines the deployment boundary of MM-RISs. Due to the non-convexity and non-linearity of the problem, as well as the mixed high-dimensional discrete and continuous variables under highly dynamic environments, solving \eqref{prob} is highly challenging. Hence, we propose an advanced DRL-based approach as detailed in the following section.
\section{Scaling-Law Analysis}
We provide theoretical insights into the scalability of the proposed MM-RIS architecture with respect to the number of MEs $M$. We characterize the scaling behaviors of the desired signal, MM-RIS-induced amplification noise, achievable rate, and EE. Assume that: 1) the element-wise channel coefficients have finite and non-zero first and second moments; 2) the MM-RIS amplification coefficients are bounded as $0\leq \beta_{q,m}^{k} \leq \beta^k_{\text{max}} < \infty$; 3) a non-vanishing fraction of the MM-RIS elements operates in the signal mode as $M$ increases; and 4) the phase-shifts of MM-RISs are configured to coherently combine the desired cascaded channel; 5) the MM-RIS aperture and ME movement velocities are bounded as $M$ increases.
\begin{proposition} \label{prop1}
For each BS-MM-RIS-user cascaded link, under coherent phase configuration, bounded amplification coefficients, and finite channel moments, the desired received signal power scales as $P_{\mathrm{sig}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$, whereas the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise power scales as $P_{\mathrm{AN}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$. When the residual interference is bounded, i.e., $P_{\mathrm{I}}(M) = \mathcal{O}(1)$, the SINR reduces to
\begin{align} \label{c1c2}
\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2}{c_1M+c_2} \right) =
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{O}(M^2), & c_1 M \ll c_2, 
\mathcal{O}(M), & c_1 M \gg c_2,
\end{cases}
\end{align}
where $c_1>0$ represents the equivalent MM-RIS amplification noise coefficient, whilst $c_2>0$ collects the receiver noise and disturbance terms. Accordingly, the communication-phase achievable rate satisfies $r(M)=\log_2(1+\gamma(M))
=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. Under bounded ME movement, the movement time overhead preserves the asymptotic rate scaling, yielding $R(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The cascaded channel through the $q$-th MM-RIS can be expressed as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k}\mathbf{H}_q \mathbf{f} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m} \sqrt{\beta_{q,m}^{k}} g_{q,kj,m}^{*} \mathbf{h}_{q,m}^{\rm T} \mathbf{f} e^{j\theta_{q,m}^{k}}$, where $\mathbf{f}$ indicates any beamforming. Under coherent assumption, $\theta_{q,m}^{k}$ compensates for the element-wise phase-shifts of the cascaded channel such that the desired components are coherently combined. Hence, $| \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k} \mathbf{H}_q \mathbf{f} |  \approx \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m} \sqrt{\beta_{q,m}^{k}}
|g_{q,kj,m}| |\mathbf h_{q,m}^{\rm T}\mathbf{f} |\triangleq f_1$. Under finite moment assumptions, bounded amplification
coefficients, and a non-vanishing fraction of elements in the signal mode, each element-wise contribution in $f_1$ has a bounded non-zero magnitude. Therefore, the coherently combined amplitude increases linearly with $M$, i.e., $f_1=\mathcal{O}(M)$, which yields $P_{\mathrm{sig}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. On the other hand, the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise associated with the $q$-th MM-RIS is proportional to $\sigma_s^2
\| \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\rm H} \mathbf{\Theta}_q^{k} \|^2 = \sigma_s^2 \sum_{m=1}^{M} \alpha_{q,m}^{2} \beta_{q,m}^{k} |g_{q,kj,m}|^2$. Since $\beta_{q,m}^{k}$ is bounded and the element-wise channel coefficients have finite moments, each term in the above summation has bounded power. Therefore, the accumulated amplification noise power grows linearly with $M$, yielding $P_{\mathrm{AN}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$. Let $P_{\mathrm{I}}(M)$ denote the aggregate residual multi-user interference power after transmit beamforming and hybrid RSMA-NOMA decoding. Combining the desired signal power, residual interference, and total noise terms yields $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2} {P_{\mathrm{I}}(M)+c_1M+c_2} \right)$. When the residual interference is bounded, i.e., $P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$, we have $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2}{c_1M+c_2} \right)$. When $c_1 M \ll c_2$, the denominator is dominated by the constant, and hence $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}(M^2)$ in \eqref{c1c2}. In contrast, when $c_1 M \gg c_2$, the accumulated MM-RIS amplification noise dominates the denominator, yielding $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}(M)$ in \eqref{c1c2}. Since the communication-stage achievable rate is $r(M)=\log_2\left(1+\gamma(M)\right)$, both $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^2)$ and
$\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(M)$ lead to $r(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. According to \eqref{eff_rate}, the effective rate accounting for ME repositioning is $R(M) = \left(1-\frac{T_{\rm mov}(M)}{T}\right)r(M) = \tau(M)r(M)$. Since the MM-RIS movement region is bounded and the ME velocities are lower bounded by a positive constant, $T_{\rm mov}(M)$ remains bounded as $M$ increases, i.e., $\tau(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. Consequently, $R(M)=\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. This completes the proof.
\end{proof}
\begin{corollary} \label{cor1}
Let the aggregate residual interference scale as $P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\rho})$, where $ 0\leq \rho \leq 2$, and let the effective total power consumption scale as $P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\delta})$, where $0\leq \delta \leq 1$ characterizes the residual element-dependent power overhead after EH. For $\rho < 2$, we have SINR $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( M^{2-\max\{\rho,1\}} \right)$, whereas $\rho=2$ yields an interference-limited regime with $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. Then, the system EE scales as
\begin{align}
\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M)
=
\frac{R(M)}{P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)}
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\mathcal{O}\left(
\frac{\log M}{M^{\delta}}
\right),
& 0\leq\rho<2,[3mm]
\displaystyle
\mathcal{O}\left(
\frac{1}{M^{\delta}}
\right),
& \rho=2.
\end{cases}
\label{EE_scaling}
\end{align}
Hence, when $\delta>0$, the EE asymptotically approaches zero, i.e., $\lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}
\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M)=0$.
For the uncompensated element-dependent overhead, i.e., $\delta=1$, the EE scales as $\mathcal{O}(\log M/M)$ for $\rho<2$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/M)$ for $\rho=2$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
From Proposition \ref{prop1}, the desired received signal power scales as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$, whereas the MM-RIS-induced amplification noise power scales as $\mathcal{O}(M)$. If the residual interference satisfies
$P_{\mathrm I}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\rho})$ owing to imperfect interference cancellation, the SINR can be expressed as $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{M^2} {M^{\rho}+M+1} \right)$. For $\rho<2$, the dominant denominator term scales as $\mathcal{O}(M^{\max\{\rho,1\}})$, yielding $\gamma(M) = \mathcal{O}\left( M^{2-\max\{\rho,1\}} \right)$. Since $2-\max\{\rho,1\}>0$ for $\rho<2$, SINR grows linearly with $M$, and then we have the achievable rate $R(M) = \log_2\left(1+\gamma(M)\right) =\mathcal{O}(\log M)$. When $\rho=2$, the residual interference scales at the same quadratic
order as the desired signal. Hence, $\gamma(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$ provides
$R(M)=\mathcal{O}(1)$. According to \eqref{power1} and \eqref{power2}, the effective total power consumption consists of the element-based control, amplification, and movement power after accounting for EH. By characterizing the uncompensated element overhead with the exponent $\delta$, the resulting effective total power can be obtained and scales as $P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)=\mathcal{O}(M^{\delta})$, with $0\leq \delta \leq 1$. Therefore, the EE defined as $\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M) = \frac{R(M)}{P_{\mathrm{tot}}(M)}$ scales as \eqref{EE_scaling}. For any $\delta>0$, $M^\delta$ grows asymptotically faster than $\log M$ or any bounded rate term. Therefore, $\eta_{\mathrm{EE}}(M) \rightarrow 0$ as $M \rightarrow \infty$. This completes the proof.
\end{proof}
Proposition \ref{prop1} and Corollary \ref{cor1} reveal the competing effects of coherent array gains, residual interference, amplification noise, and element-based power overhead. Although increasing $M$ provides an $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$ desired signal power gain, the resulting rate grows at most logarithmically when $\rho<2$ and becomes bounded in the interference-limited case of $\rho=2$. Meanwhile, any uncompensated polynomial power growth with $\delta>0$ eventually dominates the rate improvement. Accordingly, increasing the number of MEs does not necessarily improve EE monotonically, and a favorable finite operating region generally exists depending on the balance among array gains, interference, amplification noise, harvested energy, and hardware/movement overhead. This theoretical observation corresponds to the numerical results presented later, where EE initially improves with $M$ but eventually decreases as the additional power overhead outweighs the marginal communication gain.
\section{Proposed CRAFTS Framework}
\label{sec_alg}
\subsection{Multi-Agent Constrained Hybrid DRL}
We consider a multi-agent hybrid DRL framework characterized by state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space $\mathcal{A}$, and reward $\mathcal{R}$. Within this framework as illustrated in Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, each agent corresponds to either the BS or a single MM-RIS, which interacts with the dynamic environment by taking actions, receiving rewards, and updating its local states accordingly. Conventional centralized DRL methods struggle under conditions of high complexity and slow convergence. Moreover, the use of pure DQN or PPO becomes compellingly impractical, as both quantizing continuous variables into discrete ones and recovering introduce extra overhead and potential quantization errors. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a hybrid DRL architecture that incorporates both DQN and PPO modules for efficiently handling discrete and continuous action spaces. The state, action, and reward are defined as follows:
 \begin{itemize}
 \item \textbf{State:} The total state space is defined as a set of individual agent state $\mathcal{S}(t) = \{s_1(t), s_2(t), \ldots, s_Q(t), s_{Q+1}(t)\}$. Each agent state $s_q(t)$ is designed as $s_q(t) = \{\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}(t) | \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \forall j \in\mathcal{J}_k\}, \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}$ and $s_{Q+1}(t) = \{\mathbf{g}_{kj}(t) | \forall k \in \mathcal{K}, \forall j \in\mathcal{J}_k \}$ associated with the combined channel at timestep $t$. We note that index $1\leq q\leq Q$ indicates the MM-RIS agents, whereas $q=Q+1$ stands for the BS agent. The corresponding set of all agents is defined as $\bar{\mathcal{Q}}=\mathcal{Q}\cup \{\text{BS}\}$.
 \item \textbf{Action:} The action space is defined as a set of individual action $ \mathcal{A}(t) = \{ a_1(t), a_2(t), \ldots, a_Q(t), a_{Q+1}(t)\} $. For agents representing MM-RIS $q \in \mathcal{Q}$, each action $a_q(t)= \{ a_q^{\text{dis}}(t), a_q^{\text{con}}(t)\}$ is composed of both discrete and continuous components. Specifically, the discrete action corresponds to the selection of mode of each MM-RIS element, defined as $a_{q}^{\text{dis}}(t) = \{\alpha_{q,m}|\forall m \in \mathcal{M}\}$. On the other hand, the continuous action consists of amplitude, phase-shifts, MM-RIS location, element position, denoted as  $a^{\text{con}}_q(t) = \{ \beta^{k}_{q,m}, \theta^{k}_{q,m}, \mathbf{w}_q, \mathbf{r}_{q,m} | \forall k \in \mathcal{K},  \forall m \in \mathcal{M}\}$. As for the $(Q+1)$-th agent representing the BS, the output action consists of only continuous variables of beamforming, power split factor and common rate allocation, denoted as $a_{Q+1}(t) = \{ \mathbf{f}_{k}^c, \mathbf{f}_{k}^p, p_{k}^c, p_{kj}, R_{kj}^c  | \forall k\in\mathcal{K}, j\in\mathcal{J}_k\}$.
 
 \item \textbf{Reward:} 
The instantaneous shared reward is attained as the overall EE in conjunction with its constraints, given by
\begin{align} \label{rew}
	r(t) = \sum_{k\in \mathcal{K}}\sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} \frac{R_{kj}}{P_{\text{total}}}, \quad \text{ s.t. }  \eqref{prob_25b} \text{-} \eqref{prob_25i}.
\end{align}
Note that all agents share the reward feedback by the environments, i.e., $r_q(t)=r(t)$ for all $q\in\bar{\mathcal{Q}}$.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Lagrangian-based Constrained DRL}
Most existing works adopt penalty-based reward designs \cite{han}; however, tuning the associated penalty coefficients is often labor-intensive and highly sensitive to system configurations. Furthermore, employing hierarchical RL or metaheuristic approaches \cite{my_rl_yt} to optimize the hyperparameters of the primary RL framework may introduce excessive computational and training overhead. These methods also do not guarantee the satisfaction of constraints. Therefore, inspired by \cite{35}, we propose a Lagrangian-based method to iteratively guarantee the satisfaction of all involved constraints. The shared reward can be designed using the augmented Lagrangian in conjunction with the constraints as penalties, given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{rew_lag}
	\mathcal{L}_{\text{aug}}(\Xi, \boldsymbol{\nu},\boldsymbol{\mu}) &= \mathbbm{E} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(t) \right]  \!-\! \sum_{q\in \mathcal{Q}} \sum_{\ell\in \mathcal{C}} \nu_{q,\ell}  \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell} \!-\! \upsilon  \mathcal{H},
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\gamma^t\in[0,1]$ is the discount factor at episode $t$ indicating the importance of future rewards. $\mathcal{C}$ indicates the set of inequality constraints, whilst $\Xi$ means the policy of DRL. Notations of $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$ are Lagrangian multipliers standing for the penalty coefficients for inequality constraints $\mathcal{C}_{q,\ell}$ and equality constraint $\mathcal{H}$, respectively. The constraint penalties are given by
$\mathcal{C}_{q,1} = \sum_{m\in \mathcal{M}} \left[ \frac{1 - (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm r})^2 - (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm t})^2}{2} - \beta_{q,m}^{\rm r} \beta_{q,m}^{\rm t} \cos(\theta_{q,m}^{\rm t} - \theta_{q,m}^{\rm r}) \right]$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,2} =  \sum_{m\in \mathcal{M}} \left[ \beta_{q,m}^{\rm r} \beta_{q,m}^{\rm t} \cos(\theta_{q,m}^{\rm t} - \theta_{q,m}^{\rm r}) - \frac{(\beta_{q,m}^{\rm r})^2 + (\beta_{q,m}^{\rm t})^2 - 1}{2} \right]$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,3} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_k} \sum_{l\in\mathcal{L}_{kj}\setminus j} \left( \gamma_{kj\rightarrow kj}^{p} - \gamma_{kl\rightarrow kj}^{p} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,4} = \sum_{k\in \mathcal{K}}  \sum_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} \left( R^{\text{min}}_{kj} - R_{kj} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,5} = P_{q}^{\text{con}} - \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} P_{q,m}^{\text{EH}}$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,6} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} (\| \mathbf{f}_k^c \|^2+ \| \mathbf{f}_{k}^p \|^2) - P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,7} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} R_{kj}^c - \min_{j\in \mathcal{J}_k} C_{kj} \right)$
,
$\mathcal{C}_{q,8} =  \sum_{\substack{m,m'\in \mathcal{M},  m\neq m'}} \left( D - \|\mathbf{r}_{q,m} - \mathbf{r}_{q,m'}\| \right)$
,
and
$\mathcal{H} = \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \left( p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} - 1 \right)$. 
To solve the constrained DRL problem in \eqref{rew_lag}, we employ a Lagrangian relaxation-based approach \cite{42, 43} to enable agents to learn a constraint-aware policy by balancing the trade-off between network performance and operational safety. The corresponding Lagrangian primal-dual problem is derived by
\begin{align}
 \min_{\nu_{q,\ell} \geq 0, \upsilon \geq 0} \max_{\Xi} \ \mathcal{L}_{\text{aug}}(\Xi, \boldsymbol{\nu},\boldsymbol{\upsilon})
 \label{lagr}.
\end{align}
In order to solve the min-max problem in \eqref{lagr}, we adopt an alternative optimization iteratively obtaining the primal-dual solutions. That is, for each iteration, the policy $\Xi$ served as primal variables and the dual variables of $\{ \nu_{q,\ell},\upsilon \}$ tackling constraints are updated alternately. Thus, after conducting the main DRL scheme of policy $\Xi$, the dual variables can be updated by minimizing the dual subproblem of
\begin{align}
 \min_{\nu_{q,\ell} \geq 0, \upsilon \geq 0} \  \sum_{\ell\in \mathcal{C}} \nu_{q,\ell} \cdot \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell} + \upsilon \cdot \mathcal{H}.
\end{align}
The dual variables are then updated to minimize violations by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{d_update}
	\nu_{q, \ell} \leftarrow \left[ \nu_{q, \ell} + b_{q,\ell} \cdot \mathcal{C}_{q,\ell}\right]^{+}, \qquad 
	\upsilon \leftarrow \left[\upsilon + b_{\upsilon} \cdot \mathcal{H} \right]^{+},
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\{b_{q,\ell}, b_{\upsilon}\}$ indicate the learning rates of dual variables, whilst $[\cdot]^{+}$ denotes the projection onto the non-negative orthant. Different from the conventional Lagrangian methods where dual learning rates are fixed, the proposed framework adopts a joint action-multiplier optimization mechanism. The corresponding Lagrangian-based action is defined as $a_{q}^{\text{aug}}(t) = \{b_{q,\ell}, b_{\upsilon} | \ell \in\mathcal{C} \}$ for each agent $q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}$. Since all multipliers are continuous, the new action is presented as $\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t) = \{ a^{\text{con}}_q(t), a_{q}^{\text{aug}}(t)\}$.
\subsubsection{MADQN for Discrete Policy}
MADQN employs a deep neural network, termed Q-network, to approximate the Q-function $Q_q(s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)| \omega_q^{\phi})$ which estimates the expected cumulative reward for each action $a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)$ under a given state $s_q(t)$. Note that we define $\omega^{\phi}_q$ and $\omega^{\phi^{-}}_q$ as the model weights of the current network and of the target network of DQN, respectively. Based on the estimated Q-value, each agent selects its action using an $\epsilon$-greedy strategy, which balances exploration and exploitation by choosing a random action with probability $\epsilon(t)$ and by selecting the action with the maximum predicted Q-value with probability $ 1 - \epsilon(t)$. We design the decaying exploration as $\epsilon(t) =\epsilon(t-1) - \frac{\epsilon_{\text{max}} - \epsilon_{\text{min}}}{\epsilon_d}$, where $\epsilon_d$ is the decaying constant. Notations of $\epsilon_{\text{max}}$ and $\epsilon_{\text{min}}$ indicate the maximum and minimum exploration rates, respectively. To enhance training stability, MADQN incorporates two critical techniques \cite{38}: 
(i)
\textit{Experience replay buffer} stores historical trajectories with a tuple of $ (s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t), r_q(t), s_q(t+1))$, which allows the agent to sample mini-batches uniformly and eliminate temporal correlations during learning, where $s_q(t+1)$ indicates the newly observed state;
(ii) 
\textit{Target network update} is developed with its model denoted as $Q'_q(s_q(t), a_q^{\text{dis}}(t)| \omega_q^{\phi^-})$, which is periodically softly updated to provide stable DRL learning, i.e., $\omega_q^{\phi^-} \leftarrow \tau_{\phi} \cdot \omega_q^{\phi} + ( 1 - \tau_{\phi})  \cdot \omega_q^{\phi^-}$ where $\tau_{\phi}$ indicates the importance of target model of MADQN. The Q-network is then updated by minimizing the temporal-difference error, which measures the discrepancy between the predicted and the target Q-values, which is represented by 
$\mathcal{L}(\omega_{q}^\phi) = 
\mathbb{E}
\left\lbrace
\left[
y_q - Q_{q} (s_{q}(t), a_{q}^{\text{dis}}(t) | \omega_{q}^\phi)
\right]^{2}
\right\rbrace$,
where $y_q = r_q(t) + \gamma^{\text{dis}} \cdot \max_{a'} Q'_{q} (s_{q}(t+1), a' | \omega_{q}^{\phi^-})$ indicates the temporal difference target value and the discount factor $\gamma^d \in [0, 1] $ means the importance of future rewards.
Note that $r_q(t)=r(t), \forall q\in\mathcal{Q}$ is derived from \eqref{rew_lag} containing penalty constraints. Notation of $Q'_q(\cdot)$ is the Q-value of the target network of agent $q$. The parameter update via gradient descent is expressed as $\omega_{q}^\phi \leftarrow \omega_{q}^\phi - \eta^{\text{dis}} \cdot \nabla_{\omega_{q}^\phi} \, \mathcal{L}(\omega_{q}^\phi)$, where $\eta^{\text{dis}} \in [0, 1] $ presents the learning rate of MADQN.
\subsubsection{MAPPO for Continuous Policy}
The remaining continuous parameters are optimized using the PPO algorithm \cite{39}. Particularly, MAPPO adopts an actor-critic framework in a multi-agent manner, where each agent consisting of a policy network for actor and of a value network for critic. In the policy network, the neural network outputs the mean and standard deviation of a multivariate Gaussian distribution, where actions are sampled according to the current state $s_q(t)$ and policy $\pi_{\delta_q}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))$. Note that $\delta_q$ indicates the policy network parameters. To optimize the policy network, we employ a clipped surrogate objective function which is given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align} \label{loss_clip}
	\mathcal{L}^{\text{clip}} (\delta_q) 
= - {\mathbb{E}}_t & \big[ \min\big( O_q(\delta_q)\hat{A}_q(t), \notag 
&\quad \mathrm{clip}( O_q(\delta_q), 1 - \Lambda, 1 + \Lambda)\hat{A}_q(t) \big) \big], 
\end{align} 
\endgroup
where ${\mathbb{E}}[\cdot]$ is the expectation over a batch of generated trajectories, and $O_q(\delta_q) = \frac{\pi_{\delta_q}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))}{\pi_{\delta_{q,\text{old}}}(\bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}(t)|s_q(t))}$ is the probability ratio. $\mathrm{clip}(\cdot)$ indicates the clipping function which clips the change between the new and old policies within a range of $[1-\Lambda, 1+\Lambda]$ to avoid excessive policy updates. Note that $\delta_{q,\text{old}}(\cdot)$ indicates the old policy parameters. Furthermore, $\hat{A}_q(t)$ is the generalized advantage estimation (GAE) quantifying the difference between the observed outcome of each action in a state and the predicted state value $ V_{\mu_q}(s_q(t))$ by the value network, represented by
$\hat{A}_q(t) = \sum_{i=t}^{T_{\text{tr}}-t}(\gamma^{\text{con}} \lambda^{\text{con}})^{i-t} \cdot \left\lbrace [ (r(i) + \gamma^{\text{con}} V_{\mu_q} (s_q(i+1)) ] - V_{\mu_q} (s_q(i)) \right\rbrace$, where $\gamma^{\text{con}}$ and $\lambda^{\text{con}}$ indicate the importance ratio and GAE hyperparameters of MAPPO, respectively. Notation $T_{\text{tr}}$ means the length of trajectory segment. Note that $r(i)$ follows \eqref{rew_lag} containing penalty constraints. The policy is optimized iteratively by maximizing the clipped surrogate objective using gradient ascent given by $\delta_q \leftarrow {\delta_q} - \eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{a}} \cdot \nabla_{\delta_q} \mathcal{L}^{\text{clip}} (\delta_q)$, where $\eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{a}} \in [0, 1] $ represents the learning rate of the actor in MAPPO. The associated loss function of the value network is defined as 
\begin{align} \label{loss_value}
	\mathcal{L}^{V}(\mu_q) = \mathbb{E}_t [  \big( V_{\mu_q}(s_q(t)) - \hat{V}^{\text{tar}}_q(t) \big)^2],
\end{align}
where $\hat{V}^{\text{tar}}_q(t) 
= V_{\mu_q^-}\!\big(s_q(t)\big) + \hat{A}_q(t)$ and $\mu_q^-$ indicates the previous update of the value network. The parameters of value network are updated by the gradient method, i.e., $\mu_q \leftarrow {\mu_q} - \eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{c}} \cdot \nabla_{\mu_q} \mathcal{L}^{V} (\mu_q)$, where $\eta^{\text{con}}_{\text{c}} \in [0, 1] $ is learning rate for critic in MAPPO.
\subsection{Intra-Agent Bi-Directional Parametrized Sharing}
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=3in]{fig/agm3.eps}
\caption{The proposed bi-directional parametrized sharing and federated transformer architecture for intra-agent and inter-agent coordination, respectively.} 
\label{interintra}
\end{figure}
In the context of individual agent design in hybrid DRL, PPO and DQN typically select actions independently based on their respective input states. This isolated decision-making process neglects the potential interdependence and interaction between the two strategies within intra-agent structure. To address this, inspired by the single-directional sharing mechanism in \cite{my_ps, 30, 31}, we propose a bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism as depicted at bottom of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, where the details are illustrated in Fig. \ref{interintra}. The core idea is to enable the shared representation between the PPO and DQN models by exchanging features. Specifically, PPO agent utilizes the discrete action output from the DQN agent as the input of PPO, i.e., $s_q^{\text{con}}(t) = \operatorname{concat} ( s_q(t), \operatorname{vec}(a_q^{\text{dis}}(t-1)) )$, where ${\rm concat}(\cdot)$ indicates the concatenation of two vectors and ${\rm vec}(\cdot)$ vectorizes the action. Similarly, DQN agent also employ the continuous action output from PPO as the input, derived by $s_q^{\text{dis}}(t) = \operatorname{concat} ( s_q(t), \operatorname{vec}(a_q^{\text{con}}(t-1)) )$. 
Note that the parametrized sharing is only applied to the MM-RIS agents due to their hybrid discrete-continuous action structures, which improves the coordination between the two decision-making modules.
\subsection{Inter-Agent Federated Transformer} 
Considering all state features with equal importance is impractical in MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA systems since different channel conditions and communication variables may contribute unequally to the decision-making process. Therefore, we incorporate a transformer-based mechanism \cite{32, my_ojcom} to adaptively assign distinct importance weights to different state features, as depicted at top-left of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}. Accordingly, instead of directly utilizing the raw observation state, each agent first processes the state through a multi-head self-attention architecture associated with the linearly projected \textit{query}, \textit{key}, and \textit{value}, given by $Y_{\text{qu}} = W_{\text{qu}} s_{q}(t),
Y_{\text{ke}} = W_{\text{ke}} s_{q}(t),
Y_{\text{va}} = W_{\text{va}} s_{q}(t),$
where $W_{\text{qu}/\text{ke}/\text{va}}$ denote trainable projection matrices. Subsequently, the attention output is computed through the scaled dot-product operation as
\begin{align}\label{att}
B = \mathrm{Att}(Y_{\text{qu}}, Y_{\text{ke}}, Y_{\text{va}}) = \mathrm{Softmax} \left( \frac{Y_{\text{qu}} Y_{\text{ke}}^{\mathrm{T}}}{\sqrt{d_{\text{ke}}}} \right) \cdot Y_{\text{va}},
\end{align}
where $\mathrm{Att}(\cdot)$ denotes the attention operation and $\mathrm{Softmax}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{x_j}}$ represents the softmax activation function. The notation $d_{\text{ke}}$ indicates the feature dimension of the key space associated with $W_{\text{ke}}$. 
To further improve feature extraction capability and avoid the limitation of relying on a single attention representation, a multi-head attention structure is incorporated. Specifically, the transformed attention-aware state is generated by concatenating multiple attention heads, expressed as $s'_{q}(t) \!=\! \mathrm{MH}(Y_{\text{qu}}, Y_{\text{ke}}, Y_{\text{va}}) \!=\! \operatorname{concat}(B_1, B_2, ..., B_{N_{\text{he}}}) W_{\text{out}}$,
where $\mathrm{MH}(\cdot)$ denotes the multi-head attention operation, and $B_{n_{\text{he}}} = \mathrm{Att}(\cdot)$ is the attention output corresponding to the $n_{\text{he}}$-th attention head obtained from \eqref{att}. Moreover, $N_{\text{he}}$ denotes the number of attention heads, whereas $W_{\text{out}}$ is the trainable output projection matrix.
While the parametrized sharing mechanism effectively facilitates the coordination between MAPPO and MADQN within intra-agent, the lack of information exchanged between agents potentially leads to suboptimal solutions. To address the challenge, we design a decentralized coordination scheme by incorporating FL into the multi-agent system \cite{34, 41}, as shown at right of Fig. \ref{DRL_plot}, where the details are depicted in Fig. \ref{interintra}. Particularly, each agent independently maintains local DQN and PPO modules for distributed action execution. The local model parameters are then periodically uploaded to an aggregation server, which can be implemented at the edge or BS controller. Considering the distinct learning characteristics of continuous and discrete policies, the edge performs decoupled model aggregation for the PPO and DQN modules separately. The aggregation global model updates for round $t+1$ are expressed as
\begin{align} \label{fl_agg}
\omega_{\text{glo}} = 
\begin{cases}
	\frac{1}{Q} \sum_{q \in 
	\mathcal{Q}} \varsigma_q \cdot \omega_{q}, \qquad \text{if } \omega_{q}= \omega_{q}^{\phi}, 
	\frac{1}{Q+1} \sum_{q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}} \varsigma_q \cdot \omega_{q}, \quad \text{if } \omega_{q}\in\{ \delta_q, \mu_q \},
\end{cases}
\end{align}
where $\varsigma_q \in [0, 1]$ represents the importance weight of agent $q$. It is worth noticing that $\omega_q$ consists of transformer-related trainable model weights of $W_{\text{qu}/\text{ke}/\text{va}/\text{out}}$ per agent. This parallel aggregation process ensures global policy consistency across distributed agents while preserving local data privacy and reducing communication overhead. After the decoupled aggregation, the updated global parameters are broadcast to all local agents, i.e., $\omega_{q} \leftarrow \omega_{\text{glo}}$ for subsequent training and policy refinement.
\begin{algorithm}[!t]
\caption{Proposed CRAFTS Scheme}
\footnotesize
\label{alg}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\STATE \textbf{Initialization:}
\STATE \quad 1) Initialize environment and MADQN/MAPPO networks
\STATE \quad 2) Initialize transformer parameters and set
$a_{q}^{\text{dis}}, \bar{a}_q^{\text{con}}$, $\forall q\in\bar{\mathcal Q}$
\STATE \quad 3) Initialize Lagrangian multipliers $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$
\STATE \quad 4) Initialize replay buffer $\mathcal{D}_{q}$ and trajectory/mini-batch set $\mathcal{X}_{q}$
\FOR{$t = 1$ to $T$}
 \FOR{$q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}$}
 \STATE Extract attention-aware state
 $s'_{q}(t)$
 \IF{$q \in \mathcal{Q}$}
 \STATE $a^{\text{dis}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MADQN} ( {\rm concat}(s'_{q}(t), a^{\text{con}}_{q}(t-1)) )$
 \STATE $\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MAPPO} ( {\rm concat}(s'_{q}(t),a^{\text{dis}}_{q}(t-1)) )$
 \ELSE
 \STATE $\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t) \leftarrow {\rm MAPPO}(s'_{q}(t))$
 \ENDIF
 \STATE Extract $a^{\text{aug}}_{q}(t)$ from $\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t)$
 \STATE Apply joint action $a_{q}(t)=\{a^{\text{dis}}_{q}(t),\bar{a}^{\text{con}}_{q}(t)\}$
 \ENDFOR
 \FOR{$q \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}$}
 \STATE Observe $s_{q}(t+1)$ and obtain shared reward $r_{q}(t)=r(t)$
 \STATE Store transition/trajectory samples in $\mathcal{D}_{q}$ and $\mathcal{X}_{q}$
 \STATE \textbf{(MADQN Module):}
 \IF{$q \in \mathcal{Q}$}
 \STATE Sample mini-batch from $\mathcal{D}_{q}$
 \STATE Compute target Q-value and MADQN loss
 \STATE Perform gradient descent to update $\omega^{\phi}_{q}$
 \STATE Soft update target MADQN parameters
 \ENDIF
 \STATE \textbf{(MAPPO Module):}
 \STATE Compute GAE $\hat{A}_{q}(t)$ and target value
 \STATE Compute clipped actor loss \eqref{loss_clip} and critic loss \eqref{loss_value}
 \STATE Update MAPPO actor/critic parameters $\delta_q$ and $\mu_q$
 \STATE \textbf{(Lagrangian Update):}
 \STATE Update $\nu_{q,\ell}$ and $\upsilon$ according to \eqref{d_update} using $a^{\text{aug}}_{q}(t)$
 \ENDFOR
 \IF{FL aggregation round}
 \STATE Aggregate local MADQN, MAPPO, and transformer parameters according to \eqref{fl_agg}
 \STATE Broadcast global parameters $\omega^{\mathrm{glo}}$ to all agents
 \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
The overall procedure of the proposed CRAFTS scheme is summarized in Algorithm \ref{alg}. The process begins by initializing the MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA environment, the local MADQN and MAPPO networks, the transformer modules, and the Lagrangian multipliers for all agents. At each time step, the local state of each agent is first processed by the transformer-based feature extractor. For each MM-RIS and BS agent, the discrete and continuous actions are then jointly determined by MADQN and MAPPO, respectively, where the bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism exchanges the previous continuous and discrete actions between the two policy branches. In addition, MAPPO determines the continuous Lagrangian-related actions for adaptively updating the dual variables. The resulting joint actions are executed in the environment, after which the agents observe the updated states and obtain the shared reward. Subsequently, the MADQN and MAPPO parameters are updated according to their respective learning procedures, followed by the primal-dual updates of the Lagrangian multipliers. Moreover, the local model parameters are periodically aggregated through the FL mechanism and the updated global parameters are broadcast back to the agents. The above procedure is repeated until the prescribed training horizon is reached.

Fig. \ref{f.sim.1} illustrates the convergence of the proposed CRAFTS scheme in comparison with its downgraded variants and existing DRL benchmarks, including PPO \cite{my_ojcom}, DQN \cite{dqn}, hybrid DRL (HDRL) \cite{han}, and multi-agent HDRL (MA-HDRL) \cite{31}. Among the benchmarks, DQN achieves the lowest EE performance since its discrete-action structure suffers from the curse of dimensionality and lacks the capability to efficiently optimize high-dimensional continuous communication variables. Meanwhile, PPO exhibits improved convergence stability compared to DQN due to its capability to handle continuous action spaces.  Nevertheless, the absence of discrete decisions limits its ability to jointly optimize hybrid variables and leads to action quantization errors, resulting in suboptimal EE performance. Furthermore, HDRL employing a single-agent hybrid DQN-PPO structure outperforms both standalone PPO and DQN by jointly handling continuous and discrete actions. However, the centralized architecture suffers from the limited scalability and insufficient coordination in large-scale environments. In contrast, MA-HDRL further improves EE by leveraging multi-agent cooperation, enabling distributed optimization among multiple RIS agents and MEs. However, the lack of effective inter-agent knowledge sharing and feature extraction still limits its convergence efficiency and the corresponding performance. To further investigate the effectiveness of each proposed module, the variants of CRAFTS are evaluated. Specifically, CRAFTS-BiPS only incorporates the bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism without FL and transformer enhancement. By enabling mutual information exchange between the PPO and DQN branches, CRAFTS-BiPS achieves noticeable EE improvement over MA-HDRL. Meanwhile, CRAFTS-FT integrating FL and transformer achieves superior stability and higher EE compared to benchmarks. The CRAFTS accomplishes the highest EE among all baselines as it benefits from hybrid DRL, FL, transformer, and bi-directional parametrized sharing for coupled mixed actions.

\subsection{Effect of MF-RIS Elements}
\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\figsize in]{fig/Figure_4.eps}
\caption{EE performance with various MM-RIS configurations.} \label{f.sim.4}
\end{figure}
Fig. \ref{f.sim.4} compares the EE performance under different MM-RIS configurations, including cases with 
(1) fully optimized MM-RIS; 
(2) half EH capability, i.e., half elements are with $\alpha_{q,m}=0.5$; 
(3) without signal amplification $\beta_{q,m}^{k}=1$;
(4) without EH functionality of $\alpha_{q,m}=1$; 
(5) half EH and without amplification $\beta_{q,m}^{k}=1$; 
(6) without both EH and amplification; 
(7) reflection-only operation. 
The results indicate that when EH is disabled, the EE initially exhibits a slight improvement with an increasing number of elements, but subsequently declines significantly. This trend implies that additional MM-RIS elements initially provide enhanced array and beamforming gains, whereas excessive elements introduce substantially higher operational power consumption associated with movement, control, and signal amplification, which eventually dominates the achievable rate gain and degrades EE. In contrast, enabling EH provides significantly higher EE than the corresponding non-EH configurations because the harvested energy can partially compensate for the additional element-dependent power consumption and support active signal amplification. However, as the number of MM-RIS elements continues to increase, the incremental harvested energy may become insufficient to compensate for the increasing operational expenditure, resulting in a decline in EE. The crossover points among different MM-RIS configurations further reveal this competing relationship. For a relatively small number of elements, configurations with signal amplification can achieve higher EE because the amplification gain effectively compensates for severe channel attenuation and provides a substantial rate improvement relative to its additional power consumption. However, as the number of elements increases, the accumulated amplification and movement power grows, whilst the marginal communication gain gradually diminishes. As a result, configurations with partial or disabled amplification may become comparably more energy-efficient, leading to intersections among the corresponding EE curves. Similarly, EH shifts these crossover points by offsetting part of the increased operational power, allowing EH-enabled configurations to maintain their EE advantage over a wider range of element numbers. These crossings indicate that no single MM-RIS operating mode is uniformly optimal for all cases of $M$. Alternatively, the preferred configuration depends on the compelling balance among array gains, amplification gains, harvested energy, and element power consumption. For the half-EH case, the system achieves improved EE by leveraging partially harvested energy to support signal amplification with $\beta_{q,m}^k>1$, thereby outperforming its counterpart without amplification over most of the considered operating range. Without amplification, the MM-RIS behaves similarly to a passive metasurface and cannot effectively compensate for severe channel fading, resulting in reduced EE performance. Furthermore, the "No EH and No Amp." baseline generally exhibits the lowest EE among the STAR-capable MM-RIS configurations because both energy harvesting and active signal enhancement are disabled, effectively degenerating into a conventional passive STAR structure. Additionally, in the reflection-only RIS case, the transmitted signals cannot effectively serve users located on the opposite side of the surface, resulting in substantial EE degradation due to its limited half-space coverage. In contrast, the proposed MM-RIS simultaneously supports signal reflection and transmission, amplification, and EH, thereby providing full-space coverage while adaptively balancing communication enhancement and energy expenditure.

\begin{figure}[!t]

Fig. \ref{f.sim.7} depicts the EE performance under different numbers of users. We compare the proposed hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions to the existing multiple access mechanisms, including RSMA \cite{2}, NOMA \cite{44}, spatial division multiple access (SDMA), and OMA. For conventional RSMA, the private streams are decoded without SIC, whereas the common stream is decoded first and removed before decoding the intended private stream. For the NOMA benchmark, the common streams of RSMA are disabled, and only the private streams are transmitted using power-domain multiplexing with SIC. For SDMA, the SIC operation is disabled, and the users are simultaneously served through spatial transmission. Accordingly, when decoding the signal intended for $U_{kj}$, the signals intended for all other users $i\in\mathcal{J}_k$, $i\neq j$, within the same group are treated as interference without cancellation. For OMA, time-division mechanism is adopted, i.e., the available transmission time is orthogonally divided among all users, such that only one user is served within each
allocated time fraction. Note that all methods are optimized based solely on CRAFTS, differing only in their multiple access mechanisms. As the number of users increases, the EE of all mechanisms gradually decreases due to intensified inter-user interference and limited power resources in denser environments. The proposed hybrid RSMA-NOMA scheme achieves the highest EE across all benchmarks, benefiting from the synergistic integration of RSMA and NOMA. This is because RSMA effectively mitigates inter-user interference through message splitting and common-stream decoding, whereas NOMA further improves spectral efficiency via power-domain multiplexing and SIC. Comparably, pure RSMA achieves moderate EE owing to its robust interference management capability, whereas NOMA outperforms SDMA and OMA due to its higher spectral utilization. However, the performance of NOMA degrades as the SIC process becomes increasingly sensitive to interference accumulation in denser user scenarios. Meanwhile, SDMA suffers from limited spatial DoFs, whereas OMA exhibits the lowest EE due to inefficient orthogonal resource allocation. To elaborate a little further, the residual interference may take place owing to the imperfect SIC process, i.e., the term of $\iota \cdot \| \mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^p \|^2 \sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal{J}_k, i<j} p_{ki}$ exists owing to imperfect SIC, expressed in the denominator of private SINR in \eqref{SIC_decode}. Note that the residual interference coefficient is set to $\iota=0.3$. Although EE values of both hybrid RSMA-NOMA and pure NOMA transmissions decrease under imperfect SIC, the proposed hybrid multiple access still maintains substantial EE advantages and even outperforms the perfect SIC versions of standalone RSMA and NOMA. This result indicates that the message-splitting structure of RSMA effectively alleviates residual interference and suppresses SIC error propagation.

Then, EE declines as the total power consumption dominates the beamforming gains. To elaborate a little further, increasing $N$ enlarges the available beamforming DoFs and can potentially improve the achievable rate. However, the additional antennas at the BS also introduce antenna-dependent power consumption. Hence, assigning zero transmit power to an additional antenna does not completely eliminate its associated power consumption. As $N$ increases, the marginal beamforming and achievable rate gains become insufficient to compensate for the additional power consumption, resulting in the observed EE degradation beyond $N=6$. It is evident that the full optimization yields the highest EE, while omitting the optimization of specific parameters leads to noticeable EE degradation. Crucially, the configuration without optimizing BS beamforming results in the lowest EE performance of around $0.4$ bits/J as the active beamforming at BS is the fundamental prerequisite for establishing the primary link. Moreover, the random EH scheme also exhibits substantial EE degradation owing to inefficient energy allocation and insufficient harvested energy to support active component operations. Particularly, the random surface deployment has much lower EE than the case of the ME position adjustment, emphasizing the compelling importance of large-scale fading over small-scale fading. Among all schemes, the proposed CRAFTS framework achieves the highest EE performance across all antenna numbers. This superiority stems from the synergistic integration of hybrid DRL, FL, transformer, and adaptive Lagrangian optimization. Comparably, the HDRL-BiPS scheme achieves the second-best EE due to the incorporation of the proposed bi-directional parameterized sharing mechanism, enabling information exchange between continuous and discrete action branches. However, without FL and transformer enhancement, its capability to handle highly-coupled variables remains limited. Meanwhile, the conventional HDRL scheme further suffers from reduced coordination capability and weaker feature extraction, leading to much lower EE than HDRL-BiPS. Furthermore, conventional beamforming methods exhibit substantially lower EE than DRL-based schemes since they only optimize BS beamforming without jointly coordinating MM-RIS components. Interestingly, the heuristic method achieves relatively poor EE despite its iterative optimization capability. This is because heuristic search often suffers from high computational complexity and limited adaptability in dynamic environments, making them more susceptible to converging toward local optimal solutions. Finally, the random scheme achieves the lowest EE performance and serves as the performance lower bound.

The results indicate that although the proposed CRAFTS introduces a marginal increase in computational overhead due to the integration of the transformer model and FL aggregation, it maintains a competitive execution speed, demonstrating its potential for low-latency resource management. It is also observed that DQN suffers from the highest latency of $0.91$ s per step, primarily because the curse of dimensionality in the discrete action space complicates the Q-value estimation process. The modest increases in memory usage from $0.44$ MB to $1.11$ MB and execution time from $0.017$ s to $0.026$ s are justified by the enhanced feature extraction capability of the transformer module and the improved convergence robustness provided by FL. In summary, the proposed CRAFTS framework effectively balances architectural complexity with execution efficiency, making it an ideal candidate for low-latency intelligent resource management in future sustainable MM-RIS-aided networks.
\section{Conclusions} \label{sec_con}
	We have proposed an MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA architecture by deploying ME-enhanced MF-RISs to enable EE-oriented joint communication and spatial optimization under stringent QoS, power budget, and self-sustainability constraints. To solve the high-dimensional mixed discrete-continuous and non-convex problem, we have proposed a CRAFTS framework incorporating a transformer-based feature extraction architecture and a hybrid DRL structure combining MAPPO and MADQN. The FL and bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanisms are designed to enhance learning stability and improve multi-agent coordination under highly coupled optimization variables. Furthermore, an adaptive primal-dual Lagrangian-based scheme is conceived to dynamically regulate constraint violations and ensure reliable constraint satisfaction. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CRAFTS framework substantially outperforms both existing centralized and decentralized DRL benchmarks, conventional precoding methods, as well as heuristic optimization approaches. The results also reveal an important trade-off between communication enhancement and the operational overhead of ME-based systems, where excessive amplification, movement flexibility, or surface deployment may eventually increase power consumption and reduce EE performance. Moreover, the proposed MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA achieves superior EE across several system configurations, including imperfect SIC conditions, fixed-EH configurations, conventional RIS architectures, and baselines without amplification, EH, or ME optimization. To elaborate further, the proposed CRAFTS framework substantially outperforms both existing centralized and decentralized DRL benchmarks, conventional precoding methods as well as heuristic optimization approaches in the open literature.
From a practical implementation perspective, CRAFTS does not require retraining for every instantaneous channel realization. The policy can be trained offline over diverse channel and user realizations and then employed for low-latency online inference. Nevertheless, its generalization performance may degrade under substantial distribution shifts in user locations or propagation environments that are not sufficiently represented during training, in which case policy fine-tuning or retraining may be required. Furthermore, a multi-timescale implementation is more suitable for rapidly varying channels, where beamforming, power allocation, and electronic MM-RIS configurations are adapted on a relatively fast timescale, while MM-RIS deployment and ME repositioning are updated on a slower timescale according to user mobility and large-scale channel variations. Developing transfer, meta-learning, and continual learning mechanisms for rapid adaptation to previously unseen environments constitutes an important direction for future work. Furthermore, incorporating heterogeneous movement velocities, energy consumption, and reconfiguration delays of panel-level deployment and element-level repositioning into a multi timescale optimization framework constitutes an important direction for future studies.

\begin{abstract}
Hybrid precoding reduces the radio-frequency (RF) hardware burden in wideband massive MIMO-OFDM systems, but conventional optimization and deep neural network (DNN)-based approaches can incur high online complexity. This paper proposes XGB-SVD, a lightweight hybrid precoding framework that maps compact ray-tracing path parameters directly to analog beamforming codeword indices using cascade eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). The cascade captures sequential beam-selection dependencies and transmit--receive propagation correlation, while the digital precoder and combiner are obtained from the reduced-dimensional equivalent channel using singular value decomposition (SVD). Evaluations over five DeepMIMO scenarios spanning sub-6-GHz and millimeter-wave bands show that XGB-SVD consistently outperforms the considered DNN baselines and approaches simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) in several environments. Cross-scenario results further indicate improved transfer from propagation-diverse training environments, while XGB-SVD provides lower online computational and training costs than the DNN baselines.
\end{abstract}
\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Hybrid precoding, massive MIMO-OFDM, XGBoost, ray tracing, machine learning, DeepMIMO.
\end{IEEEkeywords}
\section{Introduction}
Wideband massive multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) is expected to play an important role in future sixth-generation (6G) wireless systems operating across both sub-6-GHz and millimeter-wave (mmWave) spectrum~\cite{liu2025itu}. Large antenna arrays provide substantial beamforming and spatial multiplexing gains, but fully digital architectures require one radio-frequency (RF) chain per antenna element, resulting in high hardware cost and power consumption.
Hybrid analog-digital precoding reduces the RF-chain burden by combining digital processing with an analog phase-shifter network. However, the constant-modulus constraint of the analog stage and the use of a common analog precoder across OFDM subcarriers make wideband hybrid precoding a challenging non-convex optimization problem.
Conventional hybrid precoding methods based on orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP), and alternating minimization can achieve high spectral efficiency ~\cite{ayach2014spatial,lee2015hybrid,yu2016alternating,sohrabi2017hybrid}. Nevertheless, repeated matrix operations and iterative optimization can incur substantial online complexity as the system dimension increases.
Learning-based hybrid precoding shifts part of this computational burden
from online optimization to offline training. Deep neural networks
(DNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been used to learn
the mapping from channel-domain representations to analog and digital
beamformers~\cite{elbir2019cnn,li2019deep,elbir2021family,mir2019machine}.
More recent studies have investigated low-complexity neural architectures,
cross-band channel reconstruction, and feedback-efficient hybrid precoding
~\cite{liu2025lowcomplexity,wei2026crossband,chou2026reducedfeedback}.
However, these approaches still commonly rely on high-dimensional channel
representations, explicit CSI reconstruction, neural-network inference,
or model-based feedback processing.
Physical propagation parameters provide a compact alternative to
full channel-matrix representations. Sensing-assisted communication and parametric channel estimation can
provide angles of arrival (AoAs), angles of departure (AoDs), path gains,
phases, and delays~\cite{xu2024little,wang2025sensing}, while recent integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) studies
further connect such parameters to channel modeling and hybrid
precoding~\cite{wang2025widebandisac}. These parameters can
therefore support analog beam selection without reconstructing the full
frequency-domain channel during learning-based inference.
Motivated by this observation, this paper develops a lightweight
hybrid precoding framework based on eXtreme Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost)~\cite{chen2016xgboost}. The proposed method directly maps
compact ray-tracing path parameters to discrete analog beamforming
codeword indices, while a cascade XGBoost architecture captures the
sequential dependence among beam selections and the correlation between
transmit and receive propagation directions. After analog beam
selection, the digital precoder and combiner are obtained analytically
from the reduced-dimensional equivalent channel using singular value
decomposition (SVD). Thus, the proposed framework combines data-driven analog beam
selection with model-based digital processing after RF-domain
dimensionality reduction.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{0pt}
\item We develop a physical-parameter-driven hybrid precoding framework that predicts analog beamforming codewords directly from compact ray-tracing path parameters, avoiding explicit full-dimensional channel reconstruction during the machine-learning-based analog beam prediction stage.
\item We propose a cascade XGBoost architecture that exploits both the sequential dependence of SOMP beam selection and the physical correlation between transmit and receive propagation directions.
\item We combine learned analog beam selection with reduced-dimensional SVD-based digital processing, avoiding direct regression of complex-valued digital beamforming coefficients and providing a favorable performance-complexity trade-off.
\item We evaluate the proposed framework over five DeepMIMO ray-tracing environments spanning sub-6-GHz and mmWave operation. Same-scenario, multi-stream, and cross-scenario experiments are conducted to characterize spectral-efficiency performance, computational efficiency, and transfer behavior across propagation environments.
\end{itemize}
\section{System Model and Problem Formulation}
\subsection{Wideband Hybrid Precoding Model}
We consider a wideband MIMO-OFDM system with
a hybrid precoder at the transmitter and a hybrid combiner at the receiver.
The transmitter is equipped with $N_t$ antennas and $N_t^{\mathrm{RF}}$ RF chains,
while the receiver is equipped with $N_r$ antennas and $N_r^{\mathrm{RF}}$ RF
chains. The transmitted OFDM waveform is composed of $K$ subcarriers, and $N_s$
spatial streams are conveyed over each subcarrier, where
$N_s \leq N_t^{\mathrm{RF}} \ll N_t$ and
$N_s \leq N_r^{\mathrm{RF}} \ll N_r$.
The  baseband signal transmitted over the $k$-th subcarrier $\bm{x}[k]\in\mathbb{C}^{N_t\times1}, k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ is
\begin{equation}
\bm{x}[k]
=
\sqrt{\frac{P_t}{N_s}}\,
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
\bm{s}[k],
\label{eq_tx}
\end{equation}
where $P_t$ is the total transmit power per subcarrier,
$\bm{s}[k]\in\mathbb{C}^{N_s\times1}$ is the symbol 
vector conveyed over the $k$-th subcarrier, satisfying
$\mathbb{E}\{\bm{s}[k]\bm{s}^{H}[k]\}=\bm{I}_{N_s}$.
The matrices  $\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}
\in\mathbb{C}^{N_t\times N_t^{\mathrm{RF}}}$ and 
$\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
\in\mathbb{C}^{N_t^{\mathrm{RF}}\times N_s}$
are the analog precoder and the digital precoder, respectively. The analog precoder is composed of phase shifters; thus, the entries in $\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}$
satisfy the constant-modulus constraint
$|[\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}]_{m,n}|=1/\sqrt{N_t}$,
where $[\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}]_{m,n}$ denotes its $(m,n)$th element.
The baseband received signal over the subcarrier $k$ is
\begin{equation}
\bm{y}[k]
=
\bm{H}[k]\bm{x}[k]
+
\bm{n}[k],
\label{eq_rx}
\end{equation}
where
$\bm{H}[k]\in\mathbb{C}^{N_r\times N_t}$
is the frequency response of the  MIMO channel, and
$\bm{n}[k]\sim
\mathcal{CN}(\bm{0},\sigma_n^2\bm{I}_{N_r})$
is the additive white Gaussian noise vector with noise variance
$\sigma_n^2$.
The receiver first applies an analog combiner, followed by subcarrier-dependent digital combiners.
The detected symbol vector is
\begin{equation}
\hat{\bm{s}}[k]
=
\bm{W}_{\mathrm{D}}^{H}[k]
\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}^{H}
\bm{y}[k],
\label{eq_combined}
\end{equation}
where $\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}
\in\mathbb{C}^{N_r\times N_r^{\mathrm{RF}}}$ and 
$\bm{W}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
\in\mathbb{C}^{N_r^{\mathrm{RF}}\times N_s}$ are the analog combiner and the digital combiner applied over the $k$-th subcarrier. Similarly, the analog combiner  satisfies
$|[\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}]_{m,n}|=1/\sqrt{N_r}$.

\subsection{Ray-Tracing Channel Representation}
In the ray-tracing model, a MIMO channel is represented through a finite set of
physically interpretable propagation paths.
At subcarrier $k$, the channel is modeled as
\begin{align}
\bm{H}[k]
=
\sqrt{\frac{N_tN_r}{L}}
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
\alpha_{\ell}
e^{j\varphi_{\ell}}
e^{-j2\pi f_k\tau_{\ell}}
\bm{a}_{r}
(\phi_{\ell}^{r},\theta_{\ell}^{r})
\bm{a}_{t}^{H}
(\phi_{\ell}^{t},\theta_{\ell}^{t}),
\label{eq_channel}
\end{align}
where $L$ denotes the number of propagation paths, $\ell$ is the
path index, $\alpha_{\ell}$ is the path amplitude,
$\varphi_{\ell}$ is the path phase, $\tau_{\ell}$ is the propagation
delay, $f_k$ denotes the frequency offset of subcarrier $k$ relative to the carrier frequency, and
$j=\sqrt{-1}$. The angles
$\phi_{\ell}^{t}$ and $\phi_{\ell}^{r}$ denote the transmit and receive
azimuth angles, respectively, while
$\theta_{\ell}^{t}$ and $\theta_{\ell}^{r}$ denote the corresponding
elevation angles.
The vectors
$\bm{a}_{t}(\phi,\theta)\in\mathbb{C}^{N_t\times1}$ and
$\bm{a}_{r}(\phi,\theta)\in\mathbb{C}^{N_r\times1}$
denote the three-dimensional beam-steering vectors for the uniform planar arrays (UPAs) at the transmitter and receiver, respectively.
In most existing work, the hybrid precoder is optimized based on the information of the channel matrix. To reduce the learning model size and the corresponding computational complexity, the channel information adopted in our model is replaced with a vector of the  path-domain features, which is defined by
$\bm{p}_{\ell}=
[\alpha_{\ell},\varphi_{\ell},\tau_{\ell},
\phi_{\ell}^{t},\theta_{\ell}^{t},
\phi_{\ell}^{r},\theta_{\ell}^{r}]^{T},$
for each propagation path.
The input of the proposed model is a fixed-dimensional feature representation obtained by retaining at
most the $L_{\max}$ strongest paths and stacking them as
$\bm{p}=[\bm{p}_{1}^{T},\ldots,\bm{p}_{L_{\max}}^{T}]^{T}
\in\mathbb{R}^{7L_{\max}}$.
If $L>L_{\max}$, the $L_{\max}$ strongest paths are retained, whereas
zero padding is applied when $L<L_{\max}$. In this work, the length is set as $L_{\max}=10$. Notably, the length of the learning input is independent of the number of OFDM subcarriers and UPA dimensions.
\vspace{-0.2in}
\subsection{Problem Formulation of the Hybrid Precoding Optimization}
Define the composite precoding and combining matrices as
$\bm{F}[k]=\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]$
and
$\bm{W}[k]=\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}\bm{W}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]$,
respectively. The achievable spectral efficiency is
\begin{align}
R
=&\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\log_2\det\Big(
\bm{I}_{N_s}
+\frac{\rho}{N_s}
\bm{R}_{n}^{-1}[k]
\bm{W}^{H}[k]\bm{H}[k]\bm{F}[k]
\nonumber
&\qquad\qquad\quad\times
\bm{F}^{H}[k]\bm{H}^{H}[k]\bm{W}[k]
\Big),
\label{eq_rate}
\end{align}
where $\rho=P_t/\sigma_n^2$ denotes the
transmit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
The matrix
$\bm{R}_n[k]=\bm{W}^{H}[k]\bm{W}[k]$
denotes the normalized post-combining
noise covariance matrix, while the
actual noise covariance matrix is
$\sigma_n^2\bm{R}_n[k]$.
For a fixed number of spatial streams with
equal power allocation, the reference fully
digital precoder
$\bm{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}[k]\in
\mathbb{C}^{N_t\times N_s}$
and combiner
$\bm{W}_{\mathrm{opt}}[k]\in
\mathbb{C}^{N_r\times N_s}$
are constructed from the dominant $N_s$
right and left singular vectors of
$\bm{H}[k]$, respectively.
 
The optimization of the analog precoder and digital precoders in terms of the maximal achievable rate can be expressed as follows ~\cite{lee2015hybrid}, 
\begin{subequations}
\label{precoding_problem}
\begin{align}
\min_{\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}},
\{\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]\}_{k=1}^{K}}
\quad&
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\left\|
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{opt}}[k]
-
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
\right\|_{F}^{2},
\label{precoding_objective}

\mathrm{s.t.}\quad&
\left|
[\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}]_{m,n}
\right|
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_t}},
\quad
\forall m,n,
\label{precoding_cm_constraint}

&
\left\|
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{RF}}
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
\right\|_F^2
=
N_s,
\quad
\forall k,
\label{precoding_power_constraint}
\end{align}
\end{subequations}
where $\|\cdot\|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm.
Constraint~\eqref{precoding_cm_constraint} enforces the constant-modulus
requirement of the analog phase-shifter network, while
\eqref{precoding_power_constraint} normalizes the hybrid precoder to
satisfy the transmit-power constraint at each subcarrier.
At the receiver side, the analog combiner and digital combiners can be optimized similarly based on an equivalent objective function of the squared error between the composite combiner $\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}\bm{W}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]$ and the optimal solution $\bm{W}_{\mathrm{opt}}[k]$ under the constant-modulus constraint on $\bm{W}_{\mathrm{RF}}$.
The optimization can be obtained through a SOMP algorithm~\cite{lee2015hybrid}, which incurs considerable computational complexity. To speed up the optimization procedure in the online implementation, we propose a supervised-learning-based scheme where the labels of the analog precoder or analog combiner are generated through the SOMP algorithm to ensure the resultant performance. Specifically,
the analog precoder and analog combiner are obtained separately over predefined analog codebooks based on the SOMP algorithm, and the resultant indices of the optimal codewords serve as supervised labels for the proposed learning model. The digital precoders and digital combiners are then obtained based on the SVD of the equivalent channel response, which will be discussed in Section~\ref{Sec:Precoding}.
\section{Proposed Cascade XGBoost Hybrid Precoding}
\label{Sec:Precoding}
The proposed XGB-SVD framework separates analog beam prediction from
low-dimensional digital processing. As illustrated in
Fig.~\ref{fig_framework}, physical path parameters are first converted
into a fixed-dimensional feature vector and normalized using
feature-specific scaling. Cascade XGBoost then predicts the analog
transmit and receive beams, and SVD is finally applied to the
reduced-dimensional equivalent channel.
\subsection{SOMP Label Generation}
As shown in the offline-training part of Fig.~\ref{fig_framework}, SOMP generates the analog beam-index labels used to train the cascade classifiers.
Analog beam selection is formulated as a discrete classification
problem over finite beamforming codebooks.
Let
$\mathcal{F}=\{\bm{f}_1,\ldots,\bm{f}_{N_F}\}$
and
$\mathcal{W}=\{\bm{w}_1,\ldots,\bm{w}_{N_W}\}$
denote the transmit and receive analog beamforming codebooks,
respectively, where
$\bm{f}_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_t\times1}$ and
$\bm{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_r\times1}$.
Here, $N_F$ and $N_W$ denote the corresponding codebook sizes.
The transmit and receive analog beamforming codebooks are constructed
using two-dimensional (2D) UPA discrete Fourier transform (DFT)
codebooks~\cite{ayach2014spatial} with angular oversampling to provide
finer beam resolution. Fourfold oversampling is applied along the azimuth dimension
and twofold oversampling along the elevation dimension, yielding
$N_F=512$ transmit codewords and $N_W=288$ receive codewords.
For the considered architecture,
$N_t^{\mathrm{RF}}=N_r^{\mathrm{RF}}\triangleq N_{\mathrm{RF}}$.
For each training realization, SOMP sequentially selects
$N_{\mathrm{RF}}$ transmit and $N_{\mathrm{RF}}$ receive codewords.
Let
$q_i^t\in\{1,\ldots,N_F\}$ and
$q_i^r\in\{1,\ldots,N_W\}$
denote the transmit and receive codeword indices selected at the SOMP step
$i\in\{1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{RF}}\}$.
These indices are used as supervised labels for the cascade classifiers.
\subsection{Cascade XGBoost Beam Selection}
As shown in the Cascade XGBoost beam-selection block of
Fig.~\ref{fig_framework}, the cascade is designed to capture the
sequential dependence among beam selections and the correlation
between the transmit and receive decisions.
In SOMP, each newly selected beam depends on the
residual after the previously selected beams are removed. Moreover,
AoAs and AoDs associated with the same propagation paths induce
correlation between the transmit and receive beam indices.
Let $\mathcal{G}_{i}(\cdot)$ denote the pair of transmit-side and
receive-side XGBoost classifiers at cascade stage $i$. At the first
stage, the transmit--receive beam pair is predicted directly from the
physical feature vector as
$(\hat q_1^t,\hat q_1^r)=\mathcal{G}_1(\bm{p})$.
For $i>1$, the input to cascade stage $i$ is formed by augmenting the
physical feature vector with the normalized beam indices from the
preceding stages:
\begin{equation}
\bm{z}_i=
[\bm{p}^{T},
\bar q_1^t,\bar q_1^r,\ldots,
\bar q_{i-1}^t,\bar q_{i-1}^r]^{T},
\label{eq_cascade_input}
\end{equation}
where
$\bar q_j^t=(q_j^t-1)/N_F$ and
$\bar q_j^r=(q_j^r-1)/N_W$
denote the normalized transmit and receive codeword indices,
respectively. The next beam pair is predicted as
$(\hat q_i^t,\hat q_i^r)=\mathcal{G}_i(\bm{z}_i)$,
$i=2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{RF}}$.
During training, the historical indices in $\bm{z}_i$ are the
ground-truth SOMP indices, corresponding to teacher forcing. During
online inference, they are replaced by the indices predicted at the
preceding cascade stages, resulting in an autoregressive prediction
process.
After all $N_{\mathrm{RF}}$ stages, the predicted analog beamformers
are constructed as
\begin{align}
\hat{\bm{F}}_{\mathrm{RF}}
&=
[\bm{f}_{\hat q_1^t},\ldots,
\bm{f}_{\hat q_{N_{\mathrm{RF}}}^t}],
\hat{\bm{W}}_{\mathrm{RF}}
&=
[\bm{w}_{\hat q_1^r},\ldots,
\bm{w}_{\hat q_{N_{\mathrm{RF}}}^r}].
\end{align}
The cascade therefore approximates the sequential beam-selection
structure of SOMP without executing the sparse reconstruction procedure
during online analog beam prediction.
\subsection{SVD-Based Digital Processing}
As shown in the online-inference part of Fig.~\ref{fig_framework}, SVD-based digital processing is applied after the analog beamformers have been predicted.
The proposed XGB-SVD architecture applies machine learning only to the analog beam-selection stage, while the digital beamformers are obtained analytically after RF-domain dimensionality reduction.
In contrast, the 
Fully XGB baseline uses the same physical path-parameter input and
predicts both the analog codeword indices and the digital beamforming
coefficients using XGBoost. Its analog stage follows the same cascade
beam-selection structure, whereas the digital stage is formulated as a
regression problem for the complex-valued baseband coefficients.
Prediction errors in these continuous-valued coefficients can therefore
lead to additional spectral-efficiency loss.
Given the predicted analog beamformers
$\hat{\bm{F}}_{\mathrm{RF}}$ and $\hat{\bm{W}}_{\mathrm{RF}}$, the
reduced-dimensional equivalent channel at subcarrier $k$ is
\begin{equation}
\bm{H}_{\mathrm{eq}}[k]
=
\hat{\bm{W}}_{\mathrm{RF}}^{H}
\bm{H}[k]
\hat{\bm{F}}_{\mathrm{RF}}.
\label{eq_equivalent_channel}
\end{equation}
Its singular value decomposition is
$\bm{H}_{\mathrm{eq}}[k]
=
\bm{U}_{k}\bm{\Sigma}_{k}\bm{V}_{k}^{H}$.
The digital precoder and combiner are then obtained from the dominant
$N_s$ singular vectors as
\begin{equation}
\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
=
\bm{V}_{k}(:,1:N_s),
\qquad
\bm{W}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]
=
\bm{U}_{k}(:,1:N_s).
\label{eq_digital_beamformers}
\end{equation}
Finally, $\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]$ is normalized such that
$\|\hat{\bm{F}}_{\mathrm{RF}}\bm{F}_{\mathrm{D}}[k]\|_F^2=N_s$,
consistent with the transmit-power constraint in
\eqref{precoding_power_constraint}.
\section{Simulation Results}
\subsection{Simulation Setup}
The simulations evaluate both same-scenario performance and
cross-scenario transfer using physically distinct DeepMIMO ray-tracing
environments~\cite{alkhateeb2019deepmimo}. Outdoor1, Arizona State
University (ASU) Campus, and New York City (NYC) are used as sub-6-GHz
environments, whereas Houston City and Indoor represent mmWave
environments.
The principal system parameters are summarized in
Table~\ref{tab_parameters}.

The considered benchmarks are summarized as follows.
1) \textbf{DNN-RT}: This baseline uses the same 70-dimensional
ray-tracing parameter vector as XGB-SVD and employs a DNN to predict
the analog beamforming codeword indices, followed by the same SVD-based
digital processing used in XGB-SVD~\cite{elbir2019cnn,li2019deep,mir2019machine}.
2) \textbf{DNN-H}: This baseline instead uses the reconstructed full
channel matrix as the DNN input and applies the same SVD-based digital
stage.
3) \textbf{Fully XGB}: This baseline uses the same physical
path-parameter input as XGB-SVD, but predicts both the analog codeword
indices and the complex-valued digital beamforming coefficients using
XGBoost.
4) \textbf{Fully Digital}: This benchmark employs
unconstrained fully digital water-filling over
the channel singular modes and serves as an
upper performance reference.
5) \textbf{MO-AltMin}: This method alternates between analog and digital
precoder optimization under the constant-modulus constraint
~\cite{yu2016alternating}.
6) \textbf{SOMP}: This method sequentially selects analog beamforming
codewords through sparse approximation of the fully digital precoder
~\cite{lee2015hybrid}.
7) \textbf{Random Phase}: This baseline uses randomly generated analog
beamforming phases without channel-adaptive beam selection.
8) \textbf{Random Phase+SVD}: This baseline uses random analog
beamformers followed by SVD-based digital processing on the resulting
equivalent channel.
XGBoost hyperparameters are optimized independently for each environment
using Optuna~\cite{akiba2019optuna}.
